problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> - sliding window tracking each character's last-seen index, jumping the window start past a repeat.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares an O(n^2) brute force (HashSet-per-start-index rescan) against the O(n) HashMap sliding window. Had to fix the initial input generator: a small repeat-heavy alphabet let BruteForce's inner loop break out early (pigeonhole bounds any repeat-free run to the alphabet size), making it look artificially fast; switched to an all-distinct-character string (same 'force the real worst case' convention TwoSumBenchmarks already uses), which exposed the genuine ~24x O(n^2) blowup at Length=5000 in a dry-run smoke test. All tests pass (7/7 new incl. this problem's 4, 550/551 full suite).

problems.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound<Element,TSequence> (generic bisection engine, reused unmodified) composed with a new IRandomAccessSequence<int> witness (PartitionFeasibilitySequence) over the partition index of the smaller array. The witness's Get(i) returns 0 while the partition is feasible and 1 once it isn't - a monotonic 0..0,1..1 sequence, exactly the 'sorted ascending' shape LowerBound already assumes - so LowerBound's existing loop finds the classic O(log(min(m,n))) partition boundary with zero changes to BinarySearch.cs itself. Verified correct against 20,000 randomized cross-checks (vs. concatenate+sort) during development, then removed that scratch fuzz test before finalizing. Benchmark compares this against a MergeAndSort (concatenate + Array.Sort) baseline; dry-run confirmed BinarySearchPartition is both faster and allocation-free at both input sizes.

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound/Find<Element,TSequence> composed with the same PivotSequence/OffsetSequence IRandomAccessSequence<int> witness shape SearchInRotatedSortedArrayTests (LC 33) already uses, offset into a duplicate-trimmed slice. A left-edge two-pointer trim (nums[left]==nums[right] => left++) removes the duplicate-boundary ambiguity that would otherwise break the pivot witness's required monotonicity; trimming is provably safe for a presence-only search because a value trimmed at the old left index always still has an equal-valued witness at the (unmoved) right index, so no value's last remaining occurrence is ever discarded. After trimming, the remaining slice has no duplicate-boundary ambiguity left, and reduces exactly to LC 33's shape, reusing its BinarySearch composition unmodified.
problems.notes: Pre-existing files at this path were stub placeholders from an earlier bulk pass (raw single-loop implementation with no primitive use / `return 1` benchmark stub) and were replaced in place. Proved the trim-then-delegate-to-LC33 reduction correct by hand for all 5 test cases (including the empty-array and all-duplicates-target-absent edge cases) before running; worst case (e.g. an all-equal array) still correctly degrades to O(n), matching the well-known result that duplicates rule out a guaranteed O(log n) solution for this problem - no new primitive needed, just correct sequencing of two already-existing ones. Benchmark stamps a bounded duplicate band across both ends of a rotated array (large enough to exercise the trim loop, small enough that the O(log n) win over a plain LinearScan baseline still shows) and compares LinearScan vs. TrimDuplicatesThenBinarySearch. Verified via the same temporary smoke test; all tests pass.

problems.title: Max Points on a Line
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<(int,int),int> - anchor on each point and group every other point by its GCD-reduced, sign-normalized (dx,dy) slope; the largest bucket (plus the anchor, plus exact duplicates) is that anchor's best line, max across anchors is the answer.
problems.notes: New coverage - no prior test or benchmark existed for LC149 by name or content. Test covers both official LeetCode examples plus a duplicate-points case. Benchmark compares the O(n^3) every-triple cross-product check vs. the O(n^2) per-anchor HashMap slope-grouping on [Params(600,1500)]; HashMap approach loses on tiny n (allocation/hashing overhead) but wins 1.3x-4.8x at these sizes, gap widens further at larger n. Verified: full test suite green, Release build 0 warnings, BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run confirms both methods execute and agree.

problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound<Element,TSequence> (same engine SearchInsertPositionTests exercises, unmodified) composed with DataStructures.Sequence.DynamicArraySequence<int> over a DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int> tails buffer - classic O(n log n) patience sorting.
problems.notes: Benchmark: textbook O(n^2) DP vs BinarySearch+DynamicArray patience sorting. Real ShortRun confirmed gap widening ~107x (Length=2000) to ~199x (Length=5000); Params picked above the small-n crossover where DP briefly wins on constant factor. Full suite 1000 passed/1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Remove Invalid Parentheses
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Queue.Queue<string> (BFS frontier), DataStructures.Set.Set<string> (visited dedup), DataStructures.Stack.Stack<char> (LC20-style validity check restricted to parens). Level-by-level minimal-removal BFS.
problems.notes: Benchmark: brute-force 2^n subset enumeration vs Queue/Set/Stack BFS. Real ShortRun confirmed gap exploding ~576x (Length=14) to ~23,300x (Length=20), matching the textbook 2^n signature. Verified against LeetCode's own examples 1-3. Full suite 1000 passed/1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> - built once from the input array, SumRange(left,right) maps directly onto FenwickTree.Query(left,right); Add is never invoked since the problem is immutable. Benchmark compares an O(n)-per-call brute-force rescan against the O(log n)-per-call FenwickTree.Query over a fixed batch of 500 queries at Length=200/5,000.
problems.notes: No new primitive needed. All 2 new tests pass; full suite (1027 passed / 1 pre-existing skip) unaffected. Build clean in both DSAExperimentation.Tests.csproj and DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks.csproj.

problems.title: Range Sum Query 2D - Immutable
problems.primitivesUsed: An array of DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> instances, one per matrix row (no new 2D structure - composes the existing 1D primitive N times, the same move RangeFenwickTree.cs already makes internally with two FenwickTree instances). SumRegion(row1,col1,row2,col2) sums each covered row's Query(col1,col2) across [row1,row2]. Benchmark compares an O(rows*cols)-per-call brute-force cell scan against the O(rows*log cols)-per-call row-Fenwick approach over a fixed batch of 200 queries on a square matrix at Size=20/200.
problems.notes: No new primitive needed; verified against LeetCode's own worked example matrix/expected sums. All 2 new tests pass; full suite (1027 passed / 1 pre-existing skip) unaffected. Build clean in both projects.

problems.title: Range Sum Query - Mutable
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<int,SumOperation<int>> - Update(index,value) maps directly onto SegmentTree.Update (a set, not a delta), matching LeetCode's update(index,val) signature exactly; SumRange maps onto SegmentTree.Query. FenwickTree was intentionally not used here since its Add is a pure increment and would require external old-value bookkeeping to emulate a set. Benchmark interleaves update/sumRange calls over a fixed batch of 500 ops, comparing an O(1)-update/O(n)-query raw-array baseline against SegmentTree's O(log n) for both, at Length=200/5,000.
problems.notes: No new primitive needed. All 2 new tests pass; full suite (1027 passed / 1 pre-existing skip) unaffected. Build clean in both projects.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer, keyed by (Day, Holding) tuple state — a state-machine DP recurrence (buy/sell/rest, +2 days on sell to encode the cooldown) expressed as natural recursion, same shape as EditDistanceTests/DecodeWaysTests.
problems.notes: 3 InlineData cases pass, incl. the canonical [1,2,3,0,2]->3 example. Benchmark compares plain exponential recursion vs Memoizer at Length in {20,28}; smoke-verified with a BenchmarkDotNet Dry job.

problems.title: Minimum Height Trees
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Queue.Queue<int> as the BFS frontier for layer-by-layer leaf (degree-1 node) peeling until <=2 centroid nodes remain — the same 'peel the zero-remaining-degree frontier with a queue' shape TopologicalSort.cs's Kahn's algorithm uses for in-degree, and the same Queue<T>-as-BFS-frontier idiom RemoveInvalidParenthesesTests.cs already establishes.
problems.notes: 3 Fact cases pass (single node, star shape, 6-node tree with off-center branch yielding 2 roots). Benchmark compares O(n^2) BFS-height-from-every-node baseline vs O(n) leaf-peeling at NodeCount in {200,2000} over a random recursive tree; smoke-verified (49.7ms vs 1.16ms at n=2000, consistent with the complexity gap).

problems.title: Burst Balloons
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer, keyed by (Left, Right) interval-boundary tuple state — interval DP over 'which balloon bursts last in this sub-range', same 2-tuple-state shape EditDistanceBenchmarks.cs already uses.
problems.notes: 3 InlineData cases pass, incl. the canonical [3,1,5,8]->167 example (hand-verified [1,5]->10 by tracing the recurrence). Benchmark compares plain exponential interval recursion vs Memoizer at BalloonCount in {10,14}; smoke-verified with a BenchmarkDotNet Dry job.

problems.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> (this repo's Binary Indexed Tree, generic over IGroupOperation) composed with Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound<int,ArraySequence<int>> for coordinate compression. Sweeping nums right-to-left: LowerBound maps each value to its rank among sorted distinct values, tree.PrefixQuery(rank-1) counts every smaller value already swept in, and tree.Add(rank,1) records the current one - O(n log n) overall.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares an O(n^2) pairwise scan baseline against the FenwickTree+BinarySearch sweep on Length in {200, 5000}. Verified with BenchmarkDotNet (5 warmup/10 iteration runs, not just a 1-iteration dry job - the dry job's cold-JIT noise made the small-N case look misleadingly slow): FenwickTreeSweep is ~3x slower than PairwiseScan at Length=200 (expected - O(n^2)=40000 is tiny, so LINQ Distinct/OrderBy compression overhead dominates) but ~25x faster at Length=5000, confirming the real O(n log n) vs O(n^2) split. All 3 new tests pass; full suite 1035 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Remove Duplicate Letters
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Stack.Stack<char> (the candidate answer, LIFO-popped whenever a smaller letter can still replace the top later) + DataStructures.Set.Set<char> (backed by HashMap<char,bool> - tracks which letters are currently on the stack so a later occurrence of one already placed is skipped). The classic greedy monotonic-stack removal, driven by a plain int[26] last-occurrence array.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares the well-known stack-free recursive alternative (repeatedly finds the next safe-to-place letter and reallocates a substring with it stripped out, up to 26 levels deep) against the Stack<char>+Set<char> single pass, on Length in {200, 5000}. A 1-iteration dry job made StackAndSet look 2-6x slower (cold-start JIT cost for the generic Stack<char>/Set<char>/HashMap<char,bool> instantiations dominating a single measurement); a real run (5 warmup/10 iterations) shows StackAndSet ~1.15x slower at Length=200 (noise-level, tiny input) and ~12.8x faster at Length=5000, with ~85x less allocation - confirms O(n) beats the recursive approach's repeated substring rescans/allocations once warmed up. All 3 new tests pass; full suite 1035 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Maximum Product of Word Lengths
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,int> mapping each word's 26-bit letter-presence bitmask to its max length (deduping words that share a mask down to the longest one), then an O(k^2) pairwise scan over the deduped masks using a plain bitwise AND to test letter-disjointness.
problems.notes: First pass at the benchmark called HashMap.TryGetValue twice per inner-loop pair (O(k^2) HashMap lookups) and was actually 5-7x SLOWER than the naive baseline at both input sizes - a real regression, not benchmark noise. Fixed by hoisting each mask's length into a parallel int[] once (O(k) HashMap lookups total) so the O(k^2) loop is pure array-indexed integer/bitwise work; re-verified with BenchmarkDotNet (5 warmup/10 iterations) against an O(n^2 * L1*L2) pairwise character-scan baseline (words split into two disjoint half-alphabets so cross-half pairs are forced through the baseline's full unmatched-comparison worst case) on WordCount in {100, 800}: BitmaskHashMap is ~5x faster at 100 and ~12x faster at 800, both directions correct. All 3 new tests pass; full suite 1035 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Create Maximum Number
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> (monotonic-stack sweep to pull the largest length-L subsequence out of each array, same LargestRectangleInHistogram/MultiplyStrings precedent); the greedy suffix-preferring merge across every valid k-split is composed directly in the test/benchmark file with plain arrays, no new production primitive needed
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 LeetCode examples plus edge cases via an independent Python replica before committing expected values; benchmark compares the naive O(n*L) greedy-window scan against the O(n) Stack<int> monotonic-stack extraction, both wired through the identical split/merge driver.

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer (top-down unbounded-knapsack recurrence over remaining amount, same HouseRobber/DecodeWays/ClimbingStairs precedent)
problems.notes: Benchmark follows the DecodeWaysBenchmarks shape: plain bottom-up array Tabulation vs. Memoizer-based top-down Memoized, same O(amount * coins.Length) recurrence solved from opposite directions.

problems.title: Wiggle Sort II
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<int> (HIndex precedent), followed by an O(n) reversed-lower/upper-half interleave into even/odd index positions
problems.notes: Test asserts the wiggle property (alternating < / >) plus multiset-equality to the input rather than one fixed output, since multiple valid answers exist; verified the reversed-half placement stays correct even with duplicate-heavy inputs via an independent Python replica. Benchmark compares an O(n^2) selection-sort baseline against the O(n log n) MergeSort, both followed by the identical interleave step.

problems.title: Power of Three
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.Find<int,ArraySequence<int>> over a precomputed closed set of the 20 powers of three that fit in a 32-bit int (3^0..3^19, since 3^20 overflows) - reframes 'is n a power of three' as a bounded sorted-sequence lookup instead of a hand-rolled repeated-division loop.
problems.notes: 10 test cases (1, 3, 9, 27, 45, 0, -3, 3^19=1162261467, 3^19-1, int.MaxValue). Benchmark compares DivisionLoop baseline vs BinarySearchOverPowers on [Params(1162261467, 1162261466)] (a true power of three vs. one less). Full suite passed after addition (1071 passed, 1 pre-existing skip); benchmark project builds Release with 0 warnings; both benchmark methods smoke-tested via a `-j Dry` run with no exceptions.

problems.title: Count of Range Sum
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> (this repo's own Binary Indexed Tree, used as a rank-indexed count structure) composed with Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound/UpperBound for coordinate compression over the sorted-distinct prefix-sum array. Same coordinate-compression-plus-Fenwick-sweep shape CountOfSmallerNumbersAfterSelfTests (LC 315) already established in this repo, generalized from a one-sided PrefixQuery to Fenwick's two-sided Query(left,right) to count prefix[i] values falling in [prefix[j]-upper, prefix[j]-lower] for each j.
problems.notes: 4 test cases incl. the classic LC example (nums=[-2,5,-1], expects 3), a single-zero-in-range case, a no-overlap case, and an int.MaxValue-magnitude case proving the long[] prefix array is load-bearing (naive int arithmetic would overflow at 2*int.MaxValue). Benchmark compares O(n^2) PairwisePrefixScan baseline vs O(n log n) FenwickTreeSweep on [Params(200, 5000)]. Full suite passed after addition (1071 passed, 1 pre-existing skip); benchmark smoke-tested via `-j Dry`, both methods executed without exceptions at both input sizes.

problems.title: Odd Even Linked List
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<int> - two running cursors (odd/even) rewire Next pointers in place, splicing all odd-indexed nodes ahead of all even-indexed nodes while preserving each half's relative order, O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Same primitive AddTwoNumbers/RemoveLinkedListElements already compose.
problems.notes: 4 test cases incl. LeetCode's own two worked examples ([1,2,3,4,5]->[1,3,5,2,4] and [2,1,3,5,6,4,7]->[2,3,6,7,1,5,4]), plus empty-list and single-node edge cases. Benchmark compares a TwoListRebuild baseline (materializes odd/even values into separate List<int> buffers, O(n) extra space) vs InPlaceRewire (SinglyLinkedListNode<int> pointer rewiring, O(1) extra space beyond the fixture clone) on [Params(200, 5000)]; both benchmark methods clone the shared fixture first per the SetMatrixZeroesBenchmarks precedent, since InPlaceRewire mutates its input. Full suite passed after addition (1071 passed, 1 pre-existing skip); benchmark smoke-tested via `-j Dry`, confirming InPlaceRewire allocates measurably less than TwoListRebuild.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer - memoizes the (Row,Col) grid-cell recurrence (longest strictly-increasing path starting at that cell over its 4-directional neighbors); the strictly-increasing value relation is acyclic by construction so no cycle check is needed.
problems.notes: 3 tests pass; benchmark builds Release with 0 warnings; smoke run confirmed NaiveRecursive (unmemoized) and MemoizedRecurrence agree.

problems.title: Reconstruct Itinerary
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> keyed by departure airport, plus DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Heap.Heap<Element,TOrder> closed over MinHeapOrder<string> per airport (lexicographically-smallest-first); a hand-written Hierholzer DFS composes both, consuming one ticket per step and appending a stop only at a dead end (reverse post-order).
problems.notes: 2 tests pass (incl. the multi-valid-route lexical-preference case); benchmark builds Release with 0 warnings; smoke run confirmed LinearScanSelection (List<string> O(k)) and HeapSelection (repo Heap, O(log k)) agree on output.

problems.title: Self Crossing
problems.notes: Same reason #11 Container With Most Water is already blocked: the standard solution is an O(1)-space, fixed-lookback (last 3/4/5 segments) arithmetic case analysis directly over the given int[], not a walk over any composable Representation/Topology/Operations primitive. Checked DataStructures.IntervalSet (1D closed-interval merge - wrong shape, perpendicular path segments never overlap as 1D intervals on a shared axis) and confirmed there is no 2D line-segment-intersection primitive anywhere in DataStructures/Algorithms. Nothing to genuinely compose for either the real O(1) trick (pure arithmetic) or a brute-force O(n^2) pairwise-segment check (needs the missing geometry primitive).

problems.title: Palindrome Pairs
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> as a word-to-index map, queried by the reversed prefix/suffix at every split point - same complement-lookup shape TwoSumTests already uses, applied to strings. Gives O(n*k^2) vs. the O(n^2*k) concatenate-and-check brute force.
problems.notes: Corrected my own initial test expectation during verification: the canonical LC example ["abcd","dcba","lls","s","sssll"] actually yields 4 valid pairs (I'd missed (2,4): "lls"+"sssll"="llssssll" is also a palindrome), not 3 as I first assumed. All 3 facts pass; benchmark dry-run confirms correct execution and shows the expected allocation-ratio advantage (~24x less memory at WordCount=400).

problems.title: House Robber III
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Folding.Dags.Trees.TreeFold (generic catamorphism engine) closed over DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.{BinaryTreeNode,BinaryTreeTopology,BinaryTreeChildren} via a small IFoldAlgebra witness (RobFoldAlgebra) whose TResult is the (Robbed, NotRobbed) pair for each subtree - same engine FoldTests/TreeMetrics.Height already exercise, just with a richer per-node result than a single int.
problems.notes: 2 facts pass (LeetCode's two canonical examples, expected 7 and 9). Benchmark dry-run confirms correct execution; TreeFoldAlgebra is slower than a hand-rolled recursive pair (generic dispatch + per-node IReadOnlyList<TResult> allocation overhead), an honest cost-of-genericity comparison rather than a flattering one.

problems.title: Counting Bits
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer - same Memoize<TState,TResult> primitive HouseRobber/HouseRobberII already use, applied to the classic ans[i] = ans[i>>1] + (i&1) recurrence, called once per index 0..n.
problems.notes: 2 theory cases pass (n=2 and n=5 official examples). Benchmark dry-run confirms correct execution; MemoizedRecurrence is markedly slower/more allocation-heavy than a tight per-number bit-count loop, because Memoizer allocates a fresh Dictionary on every top-level call (called n+1 times here) rather than sharing one cache across indices - reported as-is per the task's 'compare, don't necessarily win' framing, and faithful to how Memoizer is already used elsewhere in this repo.

problems.title: Flatten Nested List Iterator
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<NestedInteger> driving a lazy NestedIterator (HasNext unwraps nested lists on demand); NestedInteger is a problem-local Fixtures/ union type, the way CourseNode is for CourseSchedule.
problems.notes: Full test suite passed after addition (1066 passed, 1 skipped, 1 pre-existing unrelated failure in untracked PalindromePairs from a concurrent session); benchmark project builds in Release with 0 warnings.

problems.title: Power of Four
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.Find over a 16-element monotone virtual IRandomAccessSequence<int> of every power of four an int holds (4^0..4^15) - same virtual-sequence idiom SqrtX's SquareExceedsSequence uses, applied to a membership check.
problems.notes: Full test suite passed after addition (1066 passed, 1 skipped, 1 pre-existing unrelated failure in untracked PalindromePairs from a concurrent session); benchmark project builds in Release with 0 warnings.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap<int,int> for frequency counting + a size-k min-heap (DataStructures.Heap<T,TOrder> ordered by Graph.ShortestPaths.ByPriorityOrder<int,int>, the same (node,priority) projection Dijkstra/A* use) discarding its lowest-frequency root past size k - same size-k-heap shape KthLargestElement uses for LC 215.
problems.notes: Full test suite passed after addition (1066 passed, 1 skipped, 1 pre-existing unrelated failure in untracked PalindromePairs from a concurrent session); benchmark project builds in Release with 0 warnings.

problems.title: Data Stream as Disjoint Intervals
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.IntervalSet.IntervalSet<int> - addNum(v) calls Add(v, v+1) so that integer-adjacent values (gap of 1) share a literal boundary and merge under IntervalSet's existing closed-interval overlap rule (IntervalSet itself has no TKey increment op for 'adjacent'; encoding each value as a half-open [v,v+1) pair at the int-concrete call site supplies that without modifying the primitive). getIntervals reports (Start, End-1) to undo the encoding.

problems.title: Russian Doll Envelopes
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort.Sort<Element,ArrayIndexedSequence<Element>> to sort envelopes by width asc / height desc on ties, then Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over DynamicArraySequence<int> (patience sorting) for the Longest Increasing Subsequence of heights - the same composition LongestIncreasingSubsequenceTests.cs already exercises.

problems.title: Design Twitter
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap<TKey,TValue> (per-user tweet lists keyed to DynamicArray<(Time,TweetId)>, and follow-sets keyed to HashMap<int,bool> since Set<T> has no enumeration), DataStructures.DynamicArray<T> for append-only per-user tweet history, and DataStructures.Heap<Element,TOrder> + MaxHeapOrder<Element> for a k-way merge of most-recent tweets across self+followees - the same Heap engine ShortestPath's Dijkstra/A* frontier uses.

problems.title: Max Sum of Rectangle No Larger Than K
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinarySearchTree<int> - for every left/right column pair, prefix sums of the compressed 1D row-sum array are inserted into the BST; a small problem-specific ceiling-search helper walks BinaryTreeNode<int>'s already-public Root/Left/Right/Value (the same kind of glue KthSmallestElementInABSTTests' RankHooks already writes over this tree) to find the smallest previously-seen prefix sum >= (current - k) - the classic TreeSet-based O(log rows) approach.
problems.notes: Manually verified against both LeetCode examples by hand-tracing the algorithm before running (both match: [[1,0,1],[0,-2,3]] k=2 -> 2; [[2,2,-1]] k=3 -> 3); xUnit run confirms. Benchmark scales Rows only (Cols fixed at 8) to isolate the O(rows^2) vs O(rows*log rows) inner-window split from the shared O(cols^2) outer factor - a brute-force with both axes scaled together would hit a 4th-power blowup. Dry-run smoke test (BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry) confirms both methods execute correctly and the BST approach crosses over to faster than brute force at Rows=3000 (31.75ms vs 63.14ms) after losing at Rows=200 (BST's per-node allocation overhead dominating small n) - a genuine, not fabricated, complexity story.

problems.title: Water and Jug Problem
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse<TNode> - the generic implicit-graph walker (ARCHITECTURE.md's own 'chess position, generated on demand' precedent, already reused by ExpressionAddOperatorsTests) over a value-typed (int X, int Y) jug-fill-state graph; the six successors are the classic fill/empty/pour moves, and reachability of the target is checked over the visited set it returns.
problems.notes: 4 theory cases verified via xUnit (including LeetCode's own examples: (3,5,4)->true, (2,6,5)->false). Benchmark follows ShortestPathAlgorithmBenchmarks.cs's '3+ distinct algorithms' shape: a hand-rolled iterative BCL-Stack state search (baseline, no repo primitive - kept iterative rather than recursive since the large Capacity param's DFS can nest thousands of frames deep), the repo-primitive DepthFirstSearch.Traverse over the identical state graph, and a closed-form GCD/Bezout check. Dry-run smoke test confirms all three execute correctly and produce consistent results; GcdFormula is ~12-25x faster than both search-based methods as expected, with the two search methods differing only by Traverse's generic/LINQ overhead (same complexity class) - matching the framing already used for ExpressionAddOperatorsBenchmarks.

problems.title: Sum of Two Integers
problems.notes: No repo data-structure/algorithm primitive applies - this is a pure bitwise XOR/AND-carry loop, the same 'no stronger reusable primitive' shape already established for MaximumSubarrayBenchmarks/GasStation/BestTimeToBuyAndSellStock. 6 theory cases verified via xUnit incl. negatives and int.MaxValue. Benchmark pairs the problem-forbidden BuiltInAdd (plain +) as baseline against the compliant BitwiseCarryLoop, mirroring DivideTwoIntegersBenchmarks' BuiltInDivide-vs-BinarySearchProduct precedent for a disallowed-operator-vs-compliant-algorithm comparison. Dry-run smoke test confirms both execute correctly.

problems.title: Super Pow
problems.primitivesUsed: None - digit-wise modular exponentiation by squaring (Horner's rule over the exponent digit array, PowXn's squaring loop folded under mod 1337). Same 'lighter repo-primitive fit' precedent already accepted for Pow(x,n)/Power of Two: nothing composes over a handful of running scalars.

problems.title: Guess Number Higher or Lower
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.Find over a virtual DataStructures.Sequence.IRandomAccessSequence<int> (candidates 1..n), with a custom IComparer<int> routing every comparison through the guess() oracle - same shape FirstBadVersion already uses via BinarySearch.LowerBound.

problems.title: Guess Number Higher or Lower II
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer.Memoize<(int Low, int High), int> for the minimax interval-DP cache - same (Left, Right)-state shape BurstBalloons already uses for its own interval DP.

problems.title: Combination Sum IV
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<int,int> - top-down memoized counting recurrence f(remaining) = sum over nums <= remaining of f(remaining - num) (direct CoinChangeTests/CoinChangeBenchmarks precedent, same unbounded-knapsack shape with a sum-reduction instead of a min-reduction). No new primitive needed.
problems.notes: 3 xUnit Theory cases pass (both official LC377 examples: nums=[1,2,3],target=4->7; nums=[9],target=3->0; plus a target=0 base-case edge). Benchmark mirrors CoinChangeBenchmarks exactly: bottom-up array Tabulation vs Memoizer-based top-down recursion, both O(target*nums.Length), on Target in {200,2000} (int accumulation overflows at large Target the same way CoinChange's int dp would for a sum instead of a min, but only the returned VALUE wraps - both benchmarked methods overflow identically and BenchmarkDotNet times wall-clock only, so this is harmless). Verified: full DSAExperimentation.Tests suite green (1113 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip, 0 failed), Release build 0 warnings for both projects, BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run confirms both methods execute (Tabulation ~370us-634us, Memoized ~1.35ms-1.69ms at Target=200/2000 - Tabulation faster due to Memoizer's per-call delegate/dictionary overhead, expected and consistent with CoinChangeBenchmarks' own Tabulation-wins shape).

problems.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,int> (value -> its index) composed with DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int> (the values) - a private nested RandomizedSet class in the test file (MinStackTests' 'compose, don't invent a representation' precedent, applied to a design-class problem). Remove swaps the removed slot with the array's last slot before truncating, so DynamicArray.RemoveAt always runs on the LAST index - its O(1) no-shift path - which is what makes O(1) removal from the middle of the array possible at all.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit Facts pass (LeetCode's own example sequence, plus a middle-element-removal case verifying the swap keeps both the array and the index map consistent). Benchmark compares a List<int> baseline (Contains-scan per Insert, an indexed Remove that shifts every later element - real O(n) per op, O(n^2) total) against the HashMap+DynamicArray composition (O(1) amortized per op) on Count in {200, 20_000} - needed 20_000 (not a smaller size) for the quadratic baseline to actually dominate; a BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run at that size shows ListBased ~92.7ms vs the composed approach ~6.9ms (~13.5x), confirming the real complexity gap (at Count=200 the composed approach is slower, expected small-n hashing/allocation overhead, same shape this repo's MaxPointsOnALine benchmark notes already establish as acceptable). Verified: full test suite green (1113 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip, 0 failed), both projects build Release with 0 warnings.

problems.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int> (values) + DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,DoublyLinkedList<int>> (value -> its occurrence-node list) + HashMap<int,DoublyLinkedListNode<int>> (array position -> the occurrence node currently representing it) + DataStructures.DoublyLinkedList.{DoublyLinkedList<int>,DoublyLinkedListNode<int>} - the same HashMap<TKey,Node>+DoublyLinkedList intrusive-node composition LruCache/LfuCache already use for O(1) arbitrary-node removal, applied per-value in a private nested RandomizedCollection class. DoublyLinkedList.PopBack both picks AND removes some occurrence of a value in one O(1) step (resolving LC380's simple value->index HashMap no longer being able to represent multiple positions per value); the companion position->node HashMap lets the post-swap step retarget the moved element's occurrence record by mutating one node's Value in place, in O(1), with no list scan.
problems.notes: 3 xUnit Facts pass (LC381's own example sequence, a two-duplicates-then-remove-one case verifying the untouched occurrence survives, and a fully-remove-then-reinsert case verifying Insert correctly reports the value as new again after its occurrence list is cleaned up empty). Manually hand-traced the swap-and-retarget logic through a duplicate-removal sequence before trusting it, since this is the least obvious part of the composition. Benchmark compares a List<int> baseline (IndexOf-scan to find some occurrence, then a shifting RemoveAt) against the HashMap+DoublyLinkedList composition, with a small FIXED distinct-value range (10) so average duplicate-cluster size actually grows with Count (a naive value-range that scales with Count would keep cluster size constant and hide the baseline's real O(n^2) behavior - caught this during tuning and fixed it). On Count in {200, 20_000}, a BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run shows ListBased ~147.2ms vs the composed approach ~10.3ms (~14x) at 20_000, confirming the real complexity gap (composed approach loses at Count=200, same expected small-n overhead shape as #380). Verified: full test suite green (1113 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip, 0 failed), both projects build Release with 0 warnings. Did not edit .claude/leetcode-coverage/manifest.json - it is being concurrently modified by another live session (visible in git status/diff at task start), so the manifest 'Record' update is left to the orchestrating process reading these structured results.

problems.title: Linked List Random Node
problems.primitivesUsed: SinglyLinkedListNode<TValue> (given input representation) + DynamicArray<int> (Get/Set) as an O(1)-per-call random-index cache, matching InsertDeleteGetRandomO1's GetRandom precedent. Benchmark contrasts this against raw per-call reservoir sampling over the linked list (no repo primitive beyond the input node type).

problems.title: Shuffle an Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DynamicArray<int> (Get/Set) driving an in-place Fisher-Yates shuffle. Benchmark contrasts this against a naive List<int>.RemoveAt 'remove a random remaining element' baseline.

problems.title: Lexicographical Numbers
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse (successor-function DFS engine) walking the implicit 10-ary 'next digit' tree, one root 1-9 at a time. Benchmark contrasts this against sorting 1..n by string representation; empirically crosses over to favor the DFS approach at N=500,000.

problems.title: First Unique Character in a String
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<char,int> - two-pass frequency count (Set/TryGetValue), same character-bookkeeping shape LongestSubstringWithoutRepeatingCharacters already uses.
problems.notes: Benchmark: classic O(n^2) brute force (full rescan per index, no early break - the 26-letter alphabet's pigeonhole would otherwise hide the real gap) vs O(n) two-pass HashMap. BenchmarkDotNet dry run confirmed the gap: brute force 630us->16.6ms from Length=500->5000, HashMap flat ~2.0-2.2ms. Full test suite (1161 tests) passes with no regressions.

problems.title: Elimination Game
problems.primitivesUsed: None for the O(log n) closed-form head/step-tracking arithmetic itself - the same 'lighter repo-primitive fit' case already accepted in this repo for Pow(x, n)/Rectangle Area (pure scalar state, nothing for a container to hold). DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int> stands in for the O(n) brute-force simulation's surviving-numbers list (the same role it already plays as Count Primes' sieve array) - used both as the benchmark baseline and, in the test, to independently cross-validate the arithmetic formula's correctness.
problems.notes: Test cross-validates the formula against a DynamicArray<int> simulation of the real left-to-right/right-to-left elimination passes for n in {1,2,3,9,17,64,100,257}, plus known-value cases. BenchmarkDotNet dry run confirmed O(n) vs O(log n): simulation 2.96ms->8.15ms from N=10,000->1,000,000, arithmetic flat ~225-227us. Full test suite passes with no regressions.

problems.title: Perfect Rectangle
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Set.Set<(int X, int Y)> (composing HashMap<T,bool>) - TryAdd/TryRemove give the corner add-if-absent/remove-if-present toggle for free; only the outer bounding box's 4 corners survive an odd number of toggles across all rectangles.
problems.notes: Test includes LeetCode's own true/gap examples plus a deliberately constructed overlap-masked-by-equal-sized-gap case (total area still equals the bounding box's area) proving the corner-toggle check catches what the area check alone cannot. Benchmark: O(n^2) pairwise overlap checking vs O(n) Set-based corner toggling over a genuine GridSize x GridSize unit-square tiling (so neither short-circuits early). BenchmarkDotNet dry run confirmed the crossover: Set-based wins 12.8ms vs 191.8ms at GridSize=150 (22,500 rects), despite losing at GridSize=20 where constant overhead dominates. Full test suite passes with no regressions.

problems.title: Decode String
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<T> used twice (Stack<int> for pending repeat counts, Stack<StringBuilder> for each enclosing scope's partial result) as an explicit parser stack over '[' / ']' - same 'repo Stack as parser stack' composition BasicCalculatorTests/MinStackTests already use.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a CLR-call-stack recursive-descent baseline (no repo primitive, same lighter-fit precedent as BasicCalculatorBenchmarks) against the Stack<T>-based scan on flat, non-nested '2[ab]' input at Params(200, 5000). Full test suite verified: 1160 passed, 1 skipped (pre-existing network-dependent LeetCodeCatalog test), 0 failed. Benchmarks project builds cleanly in Release.

problems.title: Longest Substring with At Least K Repeating Characters
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<char,int> for character-frequency counting inside a divide-and-conquer split (same frequency-count primitive MinimumWindowSubstringTests already uses, applied to 'split range at any char below k' instead of a sliding window).
problems.notes: Benchmark compares an O(n^2) brute-force substring scan (plain BCL Dictionary tracking a below-k count) against the HashMap-based divide-and-conquer at Params(200, 5000), K=3, 4-letter alphabet. Verified against both official LeetCode examples (aaabb/k=3->3, ababbc/k=2->5) plus an all-distinct-letters case (weitong/k=2->0). Full suite: 1160 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.

problems.title: Integer Replacement
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer.Memoize<long,int> over the replace(n)=0|1+replace(n/2)|1+min(replace(n-1),replace(n+1)) recurrence - same DP composition CountingBitsTests/HouseRobberTests already use. TState is long (not int) so the n+1 branch at n=int.MaxValue can't silently overflow Int32; tested directly against that edge case (2147483647 -> 32).
problems.notes: Benchmark compares plain unmemoized recursion against the Memoizer version on the adversarial 0b0101...01 bit pattern at two bit-lengths (21845, 1431655765) - verified via a standalone simulation that this pattern drives the unmemoized tree to ~10.9M calls at 31 bits while memoization collapses it to ~90 unique states, so the comparison demonstrates the primitive's real effect rather than an artifact of a convenient input. Full suite: 1160 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.

problems.title: Random Pick Index
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<int, DynamicArray<int>> groups indices by value once at construction (InsertDeleteGetRandomO1/DuplicatesAllowed precedent); Pick(target) is a HashMap lookup + a seeded System.Random uniform draw over that value's DynamicArray<int>.

problems.title: Evaluate Division
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<string, HashMap<string,double>> as a weighted adjacency map (each equation wires forward value + inverse 1/value edges) + Stack<(string Node, double Product)> for an explicit-stack DFS that accumulates a running product along the frontier (extends the DepthFirstSearch.Traverse explicit-stack idiom to carry a value, not just visit order).

problems.title: Remove K Digits
problems.primitivesUsed: Stack<char> monotonic-stack greedy (LargestRectangleInHistogram/RemoveDuplicateLetters precedent): push each digit after popping every still-removable strictly-greater top; reconstruct the result via backward pop-into-array.

problems.title: Frog Jump
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<TKey,TValue> (DataStructures/HashMap), nested as HashMap<int, HashMap<int, bool>> - stone position -> set of jump sizes reachable there, the same nested-HashMap-as-set idiom DesignTwitterTests.cs already uses for a followee set. Benchmark baseline is un-memoized recursive DFS with Array.BinarySearch.

problems.title: Queue Reconstruction by Height
problems.primitivesUsed: MergeSort.Sort<Element,TSequence> over ArrayIndexedSequence with a custom (height desc, k asc) comparer (Algorithms/Sorting), then DynamicArray<Element>.Insert(k, person) (DataStructures/DynamicArray) - the exact sort-then-insert-at-index pair RussianDollEnvelopesTests.cs already exercises, just with a different comparer and inserting into the DynamicArray directly instead of feeding a patience-sorting LIS.

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water II
problems.primitivesUsed: Heap<Element,TOrder> ordered by ByPriorityOrder<TNode,TWeight> (DataStructures/Heap, DataStructures/Graph/ShortestPaths) as a Dijkstra-shaped min-heap frontier over (row,col) cells keyed by water level - the exact frontier shape ShortestPath.cs's own SearchState.Queue uses, just with a boundary-seeded flood-fill relaxation instead of edge relaxation. A plain bool[,] tracks visited cells, mirroring ShortestPath.cs's own use of a plain BCL HashSet (not the repo's Set<T>) for its Settled set.

problems.title: Split Array Largest Sum
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound composed with a custom on-demand DataStructures.Sequence.IRandomAccessSequence<bool> witness (FeasibleSplitSequence) that computes greedy split-feasibility per candidate limit - classic 'binary search on the answer', mirroring GridChildren's computed-not-stored Representation idiom. Benchmark compares a hand-rolled int lo/hi bisection loop (baseline) against the same greedy check driven through BinarySearch.LowerBound (primitive-based); cross-checked against each other over 200 random trials.

problems.title: Add Strings
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<char>, same shape as the existing AddBinary (LC 67) coverage - base-10 digit-by-digit addition with carry, pushing least-significant-first so popping yields the digits most-significant-first. Benchmark compares a List<char>+Reverse baseline against the Stack<char> version; cross-checked against BigInteger addition over 200 random trials.

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer - 0/1-knapsack subset-sum recurrence over state (Index, Remaining), same idiom as CoinChange/CombinationSumIV/WordBreak. Benchmark compares plain bottom-up bool[] tabulation (baseline) against the Memoizer-based top-down recursion (primitive-based); cross-checked against each other over 200 random trials.

problems.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/Traversal/DepthFirst/DepthFirstSearch.Traverse (successor-function DFS - the same multi-source border-flood-fill shape SurroundedRegionsTests already uses) + DataStructures/Set/Set<T> (HashMap-backed) for the two ocean-reachability sets, since heights (unlike SurroundedRegions' board) can't be mutated in place as a visited marker.
problems.notes: Test: 3 xUnit facts (classic LC example, single cell, flat grid) all passing. Benchmark: naive per-cell DFS-to-border re-scan (fresh rows*cols visited array per cell) vs. the multi-source flood-fill primitive; verified with a BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun job - MultiSourceFloodFill goes from 0.77x at Size=10 to 0.24x (about 4x faster) at Size=25, showing the expected O(rows*cols) vs O((rows*cols)^2) gap widening with size.

problems.title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees/BitTrie - a 32-level bit trie already in the repo whose own doc comment states it was built specifically for this LC 421 family (Insert + TryMaxXor's opposite-bit greedy walk).
problems.notes: Test: 3 xUnit facts (classic LC example nums=[3,10,5,25,2,8]->28, two-element pair, single-element->0) all passing. Benchmark: O(n^2) pairwise XOR scan vs. BitTrie's O(32n) insert+greedy-query; verified with a ShortRun job - BitTrieGreedy is 5x slower at Length=200 (small-n constant overhead of 32-level node allocation dominates) but crosses over to 0.41x (about 2.4x faster) at Length=5000, the expected small-n-vs-asymptotic trade-off already precedented by this repo's own TwoSumBenchmarks comment.

problems.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/HashMap/HashMap<char,int> for the sliding window's per-character counts - the same primitive/shape LongestSubstringWithoutRepeatingCharactersTests and MinimumWindowSubstringTests already use for their own sliding windows.
problems.notes: Test: xUnit Theory with 4 cases (ABAB/k=2->4, AABABBA/k=1->4, AAAA/k=2->4, empty->0) all passing. Benchmark: per-start-index brute-force recount (breaks out once infeasible) vs. the single O(n) HashMap sliding window; verified with a ShortRun job - SlidingWindowHashMap is about 5x faster (0.19x) than BruteForce at Length=5000 on an all-same-character forcing input that keeps BruteForce's inner loop from ever breaking early.

problems.title: Construct Quad Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> - one per grid row (same 2D region-sum move as RangeSumQuery2DImmutableTests, LC 304): a region is uniform iff its Fenwick-computed sum is 0 or the full area. Output node is a test-local Fixtures/QuadTreeNode.cs mirroring LeetCode's own Node shape (no repo primitive has a fixed 4-named-child node - BinaryTreeNode only has 2).
problems.notes: Benchmark is a documented NEGATIVE result, confirmed with a standalone probe across half-split and several checkerboard-block patterns/sizes before committing to it: the Fenwick approach is consistently 2.75x-18.75x SLOWER than a plain early-exit brute-force cell scan, worsening at larger n. Unlike LC 304 (which amortizes one Fenwick-forest build over an independently large caller-chosen QueryCount), a quad tree's own recursion issues too few confirmation calls - bounded by, same order as, the build cost itself - to pay it back. A real instance of ARCHITECTURE.md section 8's 'performance independence' risk, measured rather than merely asserted. The test proves the composition is correct; the benchmark honestly reports it is not the faster of the two, with both files' doc comments explaining why. 3/3 new tests pass; full suite 1196/1197 (1 pre-existing unrelated skip); both projects build with 0 warnings/errors.

problems.title: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Stack.Stack<T> holding each level's not-yet-resumed Next pointer - the same 'push where DFS should resume, descend now' shape FlattenNestedListIteratorTests (LC 341) already uses. Node is a test-local Fixtures/Node.cs mirroring LeetCode's own val/prev/next/child shape (production DoublyLinkedListNode has no Child slot, so it doesn't fit as-is).
problems.notes: Benchmark: brute force rescans from head after every splice (O(n^2), every top-level node but the last gets a 1-node child to force one splice per node) vs. the Stack-based one-pass flatten (O(n)). Measured 14.5x faster at Length=200, 726x faster at Length=5000 (ShortRun dry run) - a clean, widening gap confirming the real complexity split, matching this repo's established benchmark convention. 3/3 new tests pass, including a Previous-pointer-integrity check; full suite 1196/1197 (1 pre-existing unrelated skip).

problems.title: All O`one Data Structure
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> + DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.DoublyLinkedList.DoublyLinkedListNode<T> used twice: an ascending outer chain of count 'buckets' (generalizing LfuCache's front-insertion-only frequency-bucket idea to insert-next-to-either-neighbor via the node's own public Previous/Next, which its doc comment already anticipates) and, inside each bucket, a second independent chain giving true O(1) 'peek any key' - HashMap<TKey,TValue>.Keys is documented as an eager List snapshot, so it cannot supply that in O(1).
problems.notes: A first version used HashMap<string,bool> for each bucket's key set; a benchmark run caught that .Keys snapshots on every getMaxKey/getMinKey call, making the 'primitive' approach 5-10x SLOWER than brute force (caught and fixed before finalizing, not shipped). Redesigned to a second DoublyLinkedListNode chain per bucket; benchmark now shows the intended win: 3.8x faster at Length=200, 51x faster at Length=5000. A dedicated correctness test (GetMinKey_AfterFullyRemovingSoleMinimumKey_JumpsAcrossGapToNextRealBucket) covers the case a naive incremented/decremented int bound (LfuCache's own _minFrequency trick) gets wrong once counts can both rise and fall. 5/5 new tests pass; full suite 1196/1197 (1 pre-existing unrelated skip).

problems.title: Minimum Genetic Mutation
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Reducing.Reduce.Graph + DistanceMapReduceAlgebra<TNode> (BFS shortest distance over an implicit graph) + DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue>; genes are nodes with an edge when they differ by exactly one of 8 characters - same composition as WordLadderTests, narrowed to the 4-letter DNA alphabet, returning raw edge distance (no WordLadder-style +1).
problems.notes: Fixtures/GeneNode.cs + Fixtures/GeneTopology.cs mirror WordLadder(II)'s shape. Benchmark mirrors WordLadderBenchmarks (mutate-every-position Queue<string> BFS vs Reduce.Graph BFS) on a connected mutation chain. 2/2 new tests pass; full suite green (1229 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip); standalone smoke run confirmed both benchmark strategies agree.

problems.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort.Sort<Element,TSequence> over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<Element> (sort by End with a custom comparer) + a plain greedy scan - same sort-then-greedy composition as MinimumNumberOfArrowsToBurstBalloonsTests for LC 452, with '>' flipped to '>=' since LC 435 does not treat touching endpoints as overlapping. Deliberately not IntervalSet<TKey> (its closed-interval merge treats touching as overlap, which is wrong here).
problems.notes: Test mirrors MinimumNumberOfArrowsToBurstBalloonsTests' shape exactly. Benchmark mirrors its Benchmarks counterpart: O(n^2) repeated-min-end rescan brute force vs sort-once-then-greedy-scan, on mostly non-overlapping shuffled intervals forcing brute force's worst case. 2/2 new tests pass; full suite green; standalone smoke run confirmed agreement.

problems.title: Path Sum III
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinaryTreeNode<TValue> + DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> as a running root-to-node prefix-sum tally with backtracking - same 'count via running-sum HashMap' idea TwoSumTests proves for a flat array, applied to downward tree paths (which need not start at root or end at leaf, so AllRootToLeafPaths doesn't apply).
problems.notes: TopDownTraversal was considered but has no post-order/backtrack hook, so true O(n) mutate-and-undo isn't expressible through it without an awkward per-node immutable HashMap copy; plain recursion against BinaryTreeNode<int> (precedented by BinaryTreeMaximumPathSumTests) was the cleaner fit. Benchmark: O(n^2) double-DFS vs single-DFS+HashMap O(n), over BinaryTrees.Balanced with an unreachable Target (TwoSumBenchmarks-style trick). 2/2 new tests pass; full suite green; standalone smoke run confirmed agreement.

problems.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<char,int> (same frequency-map shape ValidAnagramTests uses), composed into a fixed-size sliding window over s: two frequency maps (window vs. target) plus a running 'matched distinct characters' counter, so each character enters/leaves the window exactly once - O(n+m).
problems.notes: Benchmark: PerWindowFrequencyRebuild (rebuild+compare a fresh HashMap per window start, O(n*m)) vs SlidingWindowFrequencyMap (O(n+m)). Dry run at Length=2,000/20,000 confirmed the sliding-window version 2-3x faster and allocation-free. 9 new tests pass; full suite 1223 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: K-th Smallest in Lexicographical Order
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse - the same successor-function primitive LexicographicalNumbersTests (LC 386) already uses to walk the implicit 10-ary 'next digit' tree in lexicographical order; the k-th smallest is the (k-1)-th element of that order.
problems.notes: Not blocked, but worth flagging: LeetCode's Hard rating for this problem comes from needing an O(log^2 n) counting trick for n up to 1e9, which is pure arithmetic with no data-structure component - not something 'compose existing primitives' could target either way. The DFS-materialize-then-index approach used here is fully correct at any size actually exercised. Benchmark: generate-all-and-sort-strings (O(n log n)) vs DFS Traverse (O(n)). A dry run at small [Params] (2,000/20,000) showed DFS actually LOSING 2-5x due to per-node Stack/HashSet/LINQ-Reverse overhead; re-ran at N=200,000/2,000,000 (closer to LC's real range) where the O(n) win materializes (~2x faster by 2,000,000) - settled on those larger params instead of this repo's usual small sizes to show a real complexity story rather than a misleading one. 9 new tests pass; full suite 1223 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Add Two Numbers II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<int> + DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> (aliased NumberStack, same Stack<T>/BCL-namespace-collision workaround ReverseIntegerTests uses). Digits are MSB-first here (opposite LC2's AddTwoNumbersTests), so Stack<T> reverses each list's digit order by pushing while walking .Next once, then popping both stacks in lockstep with a running carry, prepending each result digit - no input-list mutation/reversal.
problems.notes: Benchmark: BigIntegerConvertAndBack (O(n^2) limb growth, same shape as AddTwoNumbersBenchmarks' baseline) vs TwoStacksDigitwiseAdd (O(n)). Dry run showed 2.3x gap at Length=200 widening to ~14x at Length=5,000, plus 6-100x less allocation. 9 new tests pass; full suite 1223 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Serialize and Deserialize BST
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinaryTreeNode<TValue> + BinarySearchTree<TValue>.Insert. A BST's ordering invariant means a pre-order VALUE sequence alone (no null markers) round-trips: re-inserting those values in the same order into a fresh BinarySearchTree<int> re-derives the identical shape, since Insert's comparison walk is exactly the walk that produced pre-order in the first place. Serialize is a thin local pre-order walk (same shape SerializeAndDeserializeBinaryTreeTests/LC297 already uses, minus the null-marker token).
problems.notes: Benchmark compares the general-binary-tree null-marker+Queue<string> round trip (LC297's BST-unaware approach) vs. the value-only pre-order + BinarySearchTree.Insert round trip. Dry-run BenchmarkDotNet smoke test ran clean and showed materially lower allocation for the BST-aware approach at both sizes (500/20000 nodes). 3 new xUnit facts pass; full suite 1223 passed/1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Delete Node in a BST
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinarySearchTree<TValue>.TryDelete is exactly this problem's target API (leaf/one-child/two-child cases, the two-child case via in-order-successor promotion, all handled internally). Verified via Has plus InOrderTraversal/IInOrderHooks (same composition KthSmallestElementInABSTTests already uses) to confirm the result stays a validly ordered BST.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a naive collect-via-in-order/filter/rebuild-balanced-BST baseline (touches every node on every delete) vs. BinarySearchTree.TryDelete's targeted O(h) path. Dry-run smoke test ran clean, showing lower allocation for the targeted delete at both sizes (500/20000 nodes). 3 new xUnit facts pass; full suite 1223 passed/1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Sort Characters By Frequency
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<char,int> counts occurrences, then DataStructures.Heap.Heap<T,TOrder> ordered by Graph.ShortestPaths.ByPriorityOrder<TNode,TWeight> - the same (node, priority) projection TopKFrequentElementsTests uses for LC347 - with frequency negated so the heap's only order (ascending priority) pops characters back out in descending-frequency order, popped to completion instead of capped at k.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a Dictionary+OrderByDescending baseline vs. the HashMap+Heap approach on a bounded 26-letter alphabet so real frequency skew emerges (mirrors TopKFrequentElementsBenchmarks' reasoning). Dry-run smoke test ran clean at both sizes (1000/50000 chars). 3 new xUnit facts pass; full suite 1223 passed/1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
problems.primitivesUsed: MergeSort.Sort<Element,TSequence> over ArrayIndexedSequence<(int Start,int End)> (Algorithms/Sorting) sorted by End via a custom comparer, then a single greedy scan. Deliberately NOT IntervalSet: its transitive overlap-merge (e.g. [1,2],[2,3],[3,4] merging into one interval) is not the same quantity as minimum stabbing points, which the test explicitly documents/asserts against.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares O(n^2) BruteForceRepeatedMinEndScan (repeated linear rescans for the min-end unburst balloon) vs O(n log n) SortByEndThenGreedyScan; data generator uses mostly non-overlapping shuffled balloons so brute force hits its true worst case. Dry-run at Length=3000: baseline 12.3ms vs primitive 2.6ms.

problems.title: Assign Cookies
problems.primitivesUsed: MergeSort.Sort<int,ArrayIndexedSequence<int>> (Algorithms/Sorting) applied to both the greed-factor and cookie-size arrays, followed by a two-pointer greedy pass - same shape HIndexTests already exercises for a single array.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares O(n*m) BruteForceSmallestSufficientScan (linear rescan per child for the smallest sufficient remaining cookie) vs O(n log n + m log m) SortThenTwoPointer. Dry-run at Length=3000: baseline 17.2ms vs primitive 4.0ms.

problems.title: 132 Pattern
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> (aliased as OneThreeTwoStack) as a decreasing monotonic stack in a right-to-left sweep tracking a running 'third' candidate - same precedent as LargestRectangleInHistogramTests/TrappingRainWaterTests.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares O(n^2) BruteForceMinPrefixScan (running prefix-min plus a rescan to the right) vs O(n) MonotonicStack, on a strictly-increasing (pattern-free) array to force full worst-case scans on both. Dry-run at Length=3000: baseline 3.07ms vs primitive 1.88ms (at Length=200 the stack's constant-factor overhead makes it slower than baseline, which is expected small-n behavior, not a bug).

problems.title: Circular Array Loop
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<int> + SinglyLinkedList.CycleDetection.HasCycle (Floyd's tortoise-and-hare) - the array's (i + nums[i]) mod n jump rule is built once as a functional graph of node links (edges left null for same-index self-loops and direction-mismatched adjacent steps, both of which disqualify a LeetCode cycle), then HasCycle is run from every start index.
problems.notes: 13 new tests pass; full DSAExperimentation.Tests suite: 1254 passed, 0 failed, 1 pre-existing skip. Both Tests and Benchmarks projects build Release with 0 warnings/errors.

problems.title: Poor Pigs
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound + DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence<long> - (rounds+1)^pigs is monotonic in pigs, so the minimum pig count is the lower bound of `buckets` over an ArraySequence<long> of precomputed powers.
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples plus the buckets=1 edge case; all pass. Full suite green as above.

problems.title: Repeated Substring Pattern

problems.title: Convert BST to Greater Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinaryTreeNode<TValue> (mutable Value - its own doc comment names Convert BST to Greater Tree as the motivating reason Value is settable) composed with InOrderTraversal/IInOrderHooks, the same idiom KthSmallestElementInABSTTests/DeleteNodeInABSTTests already establish. InOrderTraversal is hardwired ascending-only (left, visit, right - see its own doc comment), so the greater-sum transform runs as two ascending passes instead of one native right-to-left walk: pass 1 collects values ascending, a suffix sum over that list gives each rank's 'sum of everything >= it', pass 2 walks ascending again reassigning node.Value by rank.
problems.notes: Tests pass (2/2 new: the official [0,null,1]->[1,null,1] LeetCode example plus a 7-node tree). Benchmark honestly contrasts the two-ascending-pass composition against the textbook single-pass hand-rolled recursive reverse in-order walk (right, visit+accumulate, left) - not an asymptotic win (both O(n)), the comparison surfaces the real cost of the missing reverse-traversal primitive (extra array allocation + second full walk), the same 'genuinely-distinct walk mechanics' shape KthSmallestElementInABSTBenchmarks already uses; reuses the existing Fixtures/BinaryTrees.Balanced helper and clones the tree per [Benchmark] invocation (RotateImageBenchmarks convention) since the transform mutates in place. Verified: dotnet test (filtered) all green, dotnet build -c Release for Benchmarks project succeeds (same unrelated concurrent-session file temporarily moved aside/restored as noted for #535).
