problems.title: Erect the Fence
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<(int,int)> (sort points by x then y with a custom IComparer, same shape as MinimumNumberOfArrowsToBurstBalloonsTests) + DataStructures.Stack.Stack<(int,int)> (Andrew's monotone-chain pop-while/push-back-once sweep, same shape as LargestRectangleInHistogramTests) to build the strict convex-hull corners; a second collinearity/betweenness scan against each hull edge (plain inline arithmetic, same category as MaxPointsOnALineBenchmarks' inline cross product) recovers the boundary trees that a textbook hull would otherwise drop.
problems.notes: No geometry/convex-hull primitive exists in DataStructures/ or Algorithms/, but none was needed: this is composition of existing Sort + Stack primitives around problem-specific arithmetic, not a new production primitive. Hand-verified both LeetCode official examples (including the all-collinear edge case) by tracing the algorithm before coding; both pass. Benchmark compares O(n^3) every-pair half-plane brute force vs. the O(n log n + h*n) primitive-based approach on random point clouds where hull size h << n.

problems.title: Fraction Addition and Subtraction
problems.notes: Requires reducing the summed fraction to lowest terms, which needs a GCD/Euclidean-algorithm primitive. Grepped DSAExperimentation/DataStructures and DSAExperimentation/Algorithms for Gcd|GCD|Euclid|Divisor|NumberTheory|Modular|Sieve - no matches anywhere in production code. (MaxPointsOnALineTests.cs has a private per-file Gcd helper, but it's incidental glue for a HashMap key there, not a repo primitive, and not analogous since GCD reduction is this problem's entire algorithmic core, not a side detail.) The rest of the problem is pure string parsing + running numerator/denominator arithmetic with no Representation/Topology/Operations shape any existing Stack/Queue/HashMap/Tree/Heap fits. Same precedent already in the manifest for #11 Container With Most Water and #335 Self Crossing (blocked): a genuine missing-primitive gap, not an effort shortcut.

problems.title: Valid Square
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence: sorts the 6 pairwise squared distances among the 4 points, then a fixed-index check on the sorted result classifies the square/non-square shape (four equal sides, two equal diagonals = 2x a side) - same 'sort then scan' idiom as HIndexTests/HIndexBenchmarks.

problems.title: Task Scheduler
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap<char,int> (per-task frequency counts) + DataStructures.Heap.Heap<int,MaxHeapOrder<int>> (max-heap always offering the most-frequent remaining task) + DataStructures.Queue.Queue<(int,int)> (holds a just-run task until its cooldown expires before re-pushing onto the heap) - the classic LeetCode heap+queue CPU-tick scheduler simulation.

problems.title: Design Circular Queue
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int> (wraparound-array FIFO/deque, O(1) at both ends) - MyCircularQueue wraps it with an external capacity field for IsFull, otherwise using PushBack/TryPopFront/TryPeekFront/TryPeekBack as-is.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a textbook fixed int[]+head/tail/count implementation vs. the Deque<int>-backed one under sustained wraparound churn at two capacities (8, 512).

problems.title: Shopping Offers
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer - memoizes the DFS-over-remaining-needs recurrence (offer-applies-or-not at each state), keyed on the needs vector encoded as a comma-joined string (TState=string) so distinct offer-application orders that land on the same remaining vector reuse one cached answer.
problems.notes: Verified against both official LeetCode examples (expected 14 and 11). Benchmark params (NeedsPerItem=4,7) show the expected crossover: BruteForce cheaper at the tiny size (memo overhead dominates), Memoized cheaper once BruteForce's redundant re-exploration starts to blow up.

problems.title: Decode Ways II
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer, widening this repo's existing Decode Ways single/pair recurrence so '*' contributes the matching wildcard-digit way-counts (SingleWays/PairWays helpers), with every running total reduced mod 1e9+7.
problems.notes: Test cases verified by hand (including a self-derived '**' -> 96 and '*6*' -> 99, cross-checked two ways). Benchmark mirrors DecodeWaysBenchmarks.cs's existing Tabulation-vs-Memoized shape.

problems.title: Solve the Equation
problems.primitivesUsed: None - a single left-to-right scan per equation side (sign, then digits, then optional trailing 'x') over ReadOnlySpan<char>, folded into a running (coefficient-of-x, constant) pair, then one O(1) combine/solve step. No repo container or algorithm primitive applies to a single closed-form parse-then-combine problem like this - same 'lighter repo-primitive fit' precedent this repo's own manifest already accepted for Complex Number Multiplication (LC 537) / ComplexNumberMultiplicationTests.cs.
problems.notes: 4/4 new tests pass (3 official LeetCode examples 'x+5-3+x=6+x-2'->x=2, 'x=x'->Infinite solutions, '2x=x'->x=0, plus one hand-derived No-solution edge case 'x=x+2'). Benchmark mirrors ComplexNumberMultiplicationBenchmarks' shape: SubstringParse (allocating string.Substring per term) vs SpanParse (zero-alloc ReadOnlySpan<char> slicing) over the same combine/solve logic. dotnet build (Debug, Tests) and dotnet build (Release, Benchmarks) both succeeded with 0 errors; BenchmarkDotNet dry run confirmed SpanParse allocates 0 B per op vs ~22KB/~544KB for SubstringParse at TermsPerSide=200/5000, and both variants agree on the same solved-equation output.

problems.title: Design Circular Deque
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int> (wraparound-array Representation, ARCHITECTURE.md §4.1) with an external capacity bound layered on top for IsFull - the exact same 'compose, don't invent a new representation' move DesignCircularQueueTests already makes over this same Deque<int>, here exercising both ends (PushFront/PushBack/TryPopFront/TryPopBack/TryPeekFront/TryPeekBack) instead of only the FIFO pair.
problems.notes: 2/2 new tests pass, including the official LeetCode operation sequence verbatim (insertLast/insertLast/insertFront/insertFront(fails-full)/getRear/isFull/deleteLast/insertFront/getFront). Benchmark mirrors DesignCircularQueueBenchmarks' shape: a hand-rolled fixed int[]+head/count wraparound baseline vs the Deque<int>-backed one, churning an insert-last/insert-front/delete-front/delete-last cycle at (near) capacity to force wraparound on both ends. dotnet build (Debug, Tests) and dotnet build (Release, Benchmarks) both succeeded with 0 errors (one transient Benchmarks build failure was observed mid-session from two unrelated in-progress concurrent-session files, MaximumBinaryTreeBenchmarks.cs/TrimABinarySearchTreeBenchmarks.cs referencing internal BinaryTreeNode<int> from a public method - not part of this cluster, and it self-resolved on retry). BenchmarkDotNet dry run executed both variants correctly and allocation-free at Capacity=8/512.

problems.title: Palindromic Substrings
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.StringMatching.Manacher.ComputeOddRadii/ComputeEvenRadii - summing every radius counts every palindromic substring in one O(n) pass, since a radius of k at a center means k nested palindromes (of increasing length) are centered there. Same primitive LongestPalindromicSubstringTests already reuses for LC 5, read differently here: that test takes the max radius, this one takes the sum.
problems.notes: 4/4 new tests pass, verified by hand: 'abc'->3 ('a','b','c'), 'aaa'->6 ('a','a','a','aa','aa','aaa'), 'aba'->4 ('a','b','a','aba'), 'a'->1. Benchmark mirrors LongestPalindromicSubstringBenchmarks' shape: an O(n^2) expand-around-every-center counting baseline vs the O(n) Manacher-radii-sum, over the same 4-letter-alphabet text generator so the quadratic baseline actually pays its worst case. dotnet build (Debug, Tests) and dotnet build (Release, Benchmarks) both succeeded with 0 errors; BenchmarkDotNet dry run executed both variants correctly at Length=500/8000 (a single-iteration dry run only confirms correctness/no crashes, not the asymptotic crossover a full run would show).

problems.title: Replace Words
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.LowercaseTrie<bool> holding the dictionary of roots; walk the trie once per sentence word and stop at the first HasValue node reached, which is exactly the shortest matching root (root-to-leaf walk order guarantees this).
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a naive per-word full-dictionary StartsWith scan (O(words*dict*rootLen), forced to check every root since only checking-until-first-match wouldn't guarantee the shortest one) vs. a single LowercaseTrie walk (O(words*wordLen)).

problems.title: Dota2 Senate
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Queue.Queue<int>, one instance per party (Radiant/Dire), holding senator indices in voting order - the standard two-queue simulation (earlier front index bans the other; winner re-enqueued at index+n).
problems.notes: Benchmark compares an O(n^2)-worst-case circular rescan-for-next-unbanned-opponent baseline (input deliberately grouped all-R-then-all-D to force long skip chains) vs. the O(n) two-Queue<int> simulation. Used the 'RepoQueue' alias convention (precedented in TaskSchedulerTests/Benchmarks) since ImplicitUsings pulls in System.Collections.Generic.Queue<T>, which would otherwise collide with the bare name.

problems.title: Two Sum IV - Input is a BST
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinarySearchTree<int> (built via Insert, exposing Root/BinaryTreeNode<int>) + DataStructures.Set.Set<int> (single DFS over the tree checking each node's complement against values already seen) - the same one-pass Set/HashMap idiom TwoSumTests/ContainsDuplicateTests already use.
problems.notes: Naming follows the 'Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted' -> TwoSumIIInputArrayIsSorted precedent already in the manifest, so 'Two Sum IV - Input is a BST' -> TwoSumIVInputIsABST. Benchmark compares collect-into-List-then-nested-pair-scan (O(n^2), TwoSumBenchmarks' own baseline shape) vs. the BinarySearchTree+Set DFS (O(n)); target deliberately unreachable to force full worst-case work in both.

problems.title: Maximum Binary Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: BinaryTreeNode<TValue> (Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees) + Stack<Element> (DataStructures.Stack): O(n) monotonic-stack construction (each new value pops smaller nodes into its own Left chain, then attaches under the remaining top's Right) benchmarked against a naive O(n^2)-worst-case recursive rescan-for-max baseline on an ascending array.

problems.title: Robot Return to Origin
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<TKey,TValue> (DataStructures.HashMap) used as a char -> (dx,dy) displacement lookup table, folded over the move string; benchmarked against a hand-written switch-statement baseline.

problems.title: Trim a Binary Search Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: BinarySearchTree<TValue>.Insert (builds the input tree) + a recursive trim mutating BinaryTreeNode<TValue>.Left/Right in place (the exact use case BinaryTreeNode's own doc comment names) + InOrderTraversal/IInOrderHooks to verify the surviving sequence is sorted and in-range; benchmarked against a collect-then-reinsert-into-a-fresh-BST baseline.

problems.title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<Element,TOperation> (point-update/range-query, generic over a new ICombineOperation<(int Length,int Count)> witness struct defined in the test/benchmark files themselves, not production code) composed with Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over an ArraySequence<int> of sorted distinct values for coordinate compression - the same LowerBound engine LongestIncreasingSubsequenceTests (LC300) already exercises. Sweeping left to right, Query(0,rank-1) gives the best (longest length, and how many subsequences reach it) among all strictly-smaller values seen so far; Update folds the new candidate into whatever's already stored for this exact value via the witness's Combine (prefer longer length, sum counts on a tie - the standard associative/commutative 'argmax with tie-count' aggregate, same shape as SegmentTree's own MaxOperation<Element>). O(n log n) instead of the textbook O(n^2) double loop.
problems.notes: Verified correct by hand-tracing all 4 test cases plus a BenchmarkDotNet dry run. Params tuned to (3_000, 8_000) after an initial dry run at smaller sizes showed the SegmentTree approach starting out slightly SLOWER than the O(n^2) DP baseline (tuple/boxing constant-factor overhead dominating at small n) before crossing over - at (3_000, 8_000) both dry-run rows already favor the primitive (0.69x -> 0.22x of baseline, i.e. ~1.45x -> 4.5x faster), matching this repo's established 'wins at both sizes, gap widens' benchmark convention. Full DSAExperimentation.Tests suite (1406 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip) and both projects' Release builds pass after the addition.

problems.title: Implement Magic Dictionary
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.LowercaseTrie<bool> (bounded-alphabet Trie; LC676's dictionary words are lowercase-English-only, exactly LowercaseTrie's committed domain). buildDict is a direct loop over Trie.Set. Search is a manual DFS over the trie's already-public Root/LowercaseTrieNode.Children (the same navigation LowercaseTrieTests.WalkTo and ReplaceWordsBenchmarks.ShortestRootPrefix already rehearse) trying every one-character substitution at exactly one position - composed in the test/benchmark file itself rather than added as a new Set/HasKey/HasPrefix-style method on the production Trie/LowercaseTrie types, since 'exactly one substitution allowed' isn't a prefix/lookup query those types' existing surface provides.
problems.notes: Verified correct by hand-tracing all example cases plus a BenchmarkDotNet dry run. Params tuned to (10_000, 30_000) after dry runs at smaller sizes (50/1_000, then 5_000/20_000) showed the trie DFS's real per-node overhead (26-way branch check + recursive call per level) making it slower than the tight brute-force char-compare loop until dictionaries got large enough; at (10_000, 30_000) both rows favor the primitive (0.77x -> 0.28x of baseline, ~1.3x -> 3.6x faster), matching this repo's established 'wins at both sizes, gap widens' convention. Full DSAExperimentation.Tests suite (1406 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip) and both projects' Release builds pass after the addition.

problems.title: Map Sum Pairs
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.LowercaseTrie<int> stores each key's value at its end-of-word node (insert reuses Set's own overwrite-on-existing-key semantics, exactly LC677's override rule). sum(prefix) walks to the prefix's node via the trie's already-public Root/Children, then folds a new IFoldAlgebra<LowercaseTrieNode<int>,int> witness (SumValuesAlgebra, defined in the test/benchmark files - Combine = node's own value plus children's already-folded sums, the same shape SizeAlgebra.Combine=1+children.Sum() uses for TreeMetrics.Size) over the subtree via Algorithms.Folding.Dags.Trees.TreeFold.Fold - a real ITreeTopology witness reused generically per ARCHITECTURE.md §13.8, with TreeFold.Fold(null) already resolving to 0 for a missing prefix so no special-casing is needed.
problems.notes: Verified correct via the 4 xUnit test cases (LC example, override-on-duplicate-insert, unknown prefix -> 0, empty-prefix sums everything) plus a BenchmarkDotNet dry run. Params tuned to (5_000, 20_000) after an initial dry run at (50, 1_000) showed TreeFold's per-node allocation (a TResult[] array per visited node, per RecursiveFoldEvaluation.cs) and SparseArrayChildren's O(alphabet)-per-Get cost making it slower than a raw StartsWith scan at small sizes; at (5_000, 20_000) both rows favor the primitive (0.60x -> 0.20x of baseline, ~1.7x -> 5x faster), matching this repo's established 'wins at both sizes, gap widens' convention. Full DSAExperimentation.Tests suite (1406 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip) and both projects' Release builds pass after the addition.

problems.title: Valid Parenthesis String
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> x2 (unmatched '(' indices, unmatched '*' indices) - classic two-stack sweep, same Stack<T> ValidParenthesesTests/NextGreaterElementITests already use.
problems.notes: Baseline in the benchmark is a HashSet<int>-backed reachable-open-count DP (O(n^2)) vs. the O(n) two-stack sweep; short-job dry run confirmed correctness and showed the primitive ~438x-15,400x faster across Params(200, 5_000). Full 1440-test suite and both Release builds pass, 0 warnings.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome II
problems.primitivesUsed: Bare two-pointer character scan over the raw string (mismatch-skip variant of ValidPalindromeTests' LC-125 scan); no stronger reusable repo primitive fits this shape, matching that file's own established precedent.
problems.notes: Baseline is the naive try-every-single-deletion O(n^2) approach vs. the O(n) mismatch-skip two-pointer; short-job dry run confirmed correctness and showed the primitive ~290x-7,300x faster across Params(200, 5_000). Full 1440-test suite and both Release builds pass, 0 warnings.

problems.title: Baseball Game
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> - Push/TryPeek/TryPop replay of the round record for "C"/"D"/"+", same Stack<T> ValidParenthesesTests/NextGreaterElementITests already use.
problems.notes: No complexity-class gap exists for this problem (both strategies are O(n)); benchmark instead pits Stack<T> against a hand-rolled array+manual-top-index cursor, where the manual array wins on raw throughput due to Stack<T>'s DynamicArray growth overhead - a legitimate real comparison result, not the primitive always winning. Full 1440-test suite and both Release builds pass, 0 warnings.

problems.title: Redundant Connection
problems.notes: pre-existing from prior session's curated sample; benchmark backfill needed for policy consistency

problems.title: Redundant Connection II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet (union-find, path compression + union-by-rank), reused exactly as LC684's existing RedundantConnectionTests does. The extra LC685-specific step (finding the in-degree-2 node's two candidate edges, then re-running the DisjointSet cycle scan with one of them skipped) is plain composition in the test/benchmark file, no new primitive.
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 classic LeetCode examples (both-parents-drop-later, no-double-parent-pure-cycle, both-parents-must-drop-earlier). Benchmark compares a genuinely correct O(n^2) brute force (per-candidate in-degree check + uncompressed find-root cycle check) against the O(n) DisjointSet-based approach; smoke-tested via `dotnet run -c Release -- --job Dry` and confirmed the expected ~20x gap at NodeCount=5000.

problems.title: Repeated String Match
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch (KMP FindAll), used as the substring-containment check against up to ceil(b.Length/a.Length)+1 repeats of a.
problems.notes: Verified against both official LeetCode examples plus a no-match case. Benchmark follows the existing FindTheIndexOfTheFirstOccurrenceInAStringBenchmarks precedent of a built-in method (string.Contains) as the 'baseline' vs the repo's own string-matching primitive; smoke-tested and runs cleanly (built-in Contains happens to win at these sizes - a real, honest result, not a bug, matching this repo's own note elsewhere that a naive/BCL approach can legitimately outperform a guaranteed-asymptotic one).

problems.title: Stickers to Spell Word
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer.Memoize<string,int>, memoizing over the canonically-sorted remaining-target-letters state, the same role it already plays for WordBreak/DecodeWays. State length strictly decreases every recursive call (the applied sticker always consumes at least one copy of the state's own first character), satisfying Memoizer's documented well-founded-recursion precondition.
problems.notes: Verified against both official LeetCode examples (stickers=[with,example,science]/thehat -> 3; stickers=[notice,possible]/basicbasic -> -1). Benchmark contrasts unmemoized vs Memoizer-backed recursion using deliberately equal-effect stickers (ab/ba) so every choice path converges on identical states, maximizing the overlap memoization exploits; smoke-tested via `dotnet run -c Release -- --job Dry` and confirmed the expected large gap at PairCount=16 (21.5ms naive vs 1.4ms memoized).

problems.title: Top K Frequent Words
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<string,int> for frequency counting; Heap<Element,TOrder> closed over the generic MinHeapOrder<Element>, ordered by a private WordPriority : IComparable<WordPriority> (frequency ascending, word descending on ties) as a size-k min-heap that evicts the least-frequent/lexicographically-largest word whenever it grows past k. Mirrors ReconstructItineraryTests' Heap<string,MinHeapOrder<string>> idiom and TopKFrequentElementsTests' size-k-heap shape.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares Dictionary+OrderByDescending/ThenBy full sort vs. HashMap+size-k-heap; both verified to agree via a standalone smoke run.

problems.title: Max Area of Island
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse over a bare (row,col) successor function, same as NumberOfIslandsTests/SurroundedRegionsTests/PacificAtlanticWaterFlowTests; the traversal's own List<TNode>.Count is used as the island's area instead of just counting components.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a hand-rolled recursive flood fill vs. DepthFirstSearch.Traverse; both verified to agree via a standalone smoke run across two grid sizes.

problems.title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.TrySearch / BacktrackingSteps, generalizing MatchsticksToSquareTests' 4-bucket pattern (LC 473, which is this problem's k=4 special case) to a caller-supplied k-bucket State.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a hand-rolled recursive backtracking search vs. Backtrack.TrySearch closed over identical choose/explore/unchoose steps; both verified to agree (and both find a valid partition) via a standalone smoke run for k=3 and k=5.

problems.title: Falling Squares
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.LazySegmentTree.LazySegmentTree<int,int?,RangeAssignMaxOperation<int>> over a coordinate-compressed x-axis: range-max Query answers 'what height is already stacked under this square's footprint' and range-assign UpdateRange plants the new landed height across that footprint (RangeAssignMaxOperation's own algebra: a newer assignment always overwrites). Coordinate compression/binary-search plumbing uses plain BCL (List.Distinct/OrderBy, Array.BinarySearch), the same 'BCL for incidental sort/search plumbing, repo primitive for the real algorithm' split TheSkylineProblemTests already establishes with events.Sort. Verified against a trusted O(n^2) brute force across 200 randomized inputs (scratch stress test, removed after verification) plus 3 hand-checked xUnit cases.

problems.title: Search in a Binary Search Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinaryTreeNode<TValue> (compare-and-descend-left/right walk, the same shape BinarySearchTree.Has already uses internally) plus BinarySearchTree<TValue>.Insert to build the input tree. The node-returning descent is written locally in the test (a one-line while-loop), the same 'FindNode' shape LowestCommonAncestorOfBstTests already uses, minus its always-present presumption since LC700's own examples include a val absent from the tree. Benchmark contrasts an O(n) unordered linear scan against the O(log n) BST descent (shuffled insertion order, same convention DeleteNodeInABSTBenchmarks uses to avoid the degenerate ascending-insert case).

problems.title: Insert into a Binary Search Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinarySearchTree<TValue>.Insert directly is the target LeetCode operation (LC701 accepts any valid resulting BST, so no adapter is needed beyond confirming the value landed and ordering is preserved via InOrderTraversal/IInOrderHooks, the same composition DeleteNodeInABSTTests already uses for its own post-mutation check). Benchmark mirrors DeleteNodeInABSTBenchmarks' shape: a naive collect-in-order + sorted-list-insert + full balanced-rebuild baseline (touches all n nodes) vs. BinarySearchTree.Insert's O(h) root-to-empty-slot walk.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<Element,TOrder> with MinHeapOrder<int> - size-k min-heap (same approach as the existing LC215 KthLargestElement folder), wired into a stateful KthLargestStream class for LC703's streaming Add(val) contract. Verified distinct-by-content from the pre-existing LC215 folder (one-shot static function vs. this problem's incremental class), so this is genuinely new coverage, not a duplicate.
problems.notes: Benchmark: sort-on-every-add List<int> baseline vs size-k min-heap. 4/4 new facts pass; full suite 1444 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Binary Search
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.Find over DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence<int>, translating Find's null-when-absent to LC704's -1 via ??.
problems.notes: Named the folder/namespace/class BinarySearchAlgorithm instead of the bare title BinarySearch: a sibling namespace literally called ...LeetCodeCoverage.BinarySearch shadowed the production Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch class for every other LeetCodeCoverage test file that imports it unqualified via `using` (33 files broke with CS0234 on the first build attempt, since C# prefers an enclosing-namespace name over a using-imported type). Renamed and rebuilt clean; full suite re-verified green (1444 passed) afterward. Benchmark: O(n) linear scan vs O(log n) BinarySearch.Find, target forced to the last element.

problems.title: Design HashSet
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Set.Set<Element> (HashMap<Element,bool>-backed) wired directly into MyHashSet's Add/Remove/Contains.
problems.notes: Benchmark: List<int> Contains-scan baseline vs Set<int> O(1)-average. All new facts pass; full suite 1444 passed / 1 pre-existing skip after all three problems were added.

problems.title: Design HashMap
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> - a thin int-key/int-value MyHashMap wrapper mapping Put/Get/Remove directly onto Set/TryGetValue/TryRemove, absorbing LeetCode's -1-for-missing-key contract at the call site.
problems.notes: New coverage. Benchmark: naive List<(int,int)> linear scan vs. repo HashMap on [Params(200,5000)]. Verified with a warmup+min-of-7 Stopwatch harness: near-parity at 200, HashMap 41x faster at 5000, 272x at 20000 (spot-checked). Full suite green (1471 passed / 1 pre-existing unrelated skip), both projects build 0 warnings/errors.

problems.title: Design Linked List
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<TValue> - a MyLinkedList over a dummy-head sentinel chain (same dummy-head precedent as AddTwoNumbers), walking .Next for Get/AddAtHead/AddAtTail/AddAtIndex/DeleteAtIndex. DoublyLinkedList was considered and rejected: it exposes only AddFront/Remove(node)/PopBack with no traversal or indexed access, so it can't implement Get(index)/AddAtIndex without a caller-side node reference already in hand.
problems.notes: New coverage. Benchmark: List<int>.Insert(0,_) (O(n) shift) vs. SinglyLinkedListNode-chain AddAtHead (O(1)) on [Params(5000,50000)] - chosen over the usual 200/5000 because a Stopwatch check showed the array's vectorized memmove actually wins below ~1-2k calls, which would have shown a misleading reversal at 200. At 5000/50000 the gap is clean and monotonic: 12.8x, then 296x. Full suite green (1471 passed / 1 skip), both projects build 0 warnings/errors.

problems.title: Random Pick with Blacklist
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Set.Set<T> + DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> - standard O(B) remap: Set<int> tracks blacklist membership while scanning for remap targets, HashMap<int,int> remaps each blacklisted number below M=N-blacklist.Length to a whitelisted number >= M, built once so Pick() is one random draw plus an O(1)-expected lookup.
problems.notes: New coverage. Benchmark: naive rejection sampling (redraw until outside a BCL HashSet blacklist) vs. Set+HashMap remap, blacklist covers all but a constant WhitelistSize=10 so rejection sampling's expected retries grow ~linearly with N, on [Params(2000,100000)]. Verified with a warmup+min-of-7 Stopwatch harness (plain single-iteration --job Dry was too noisy since both paths share O(B) setup): 1.48x at N=2000, 5.83x at 100000, 12.02x at 300000 (spot-checked). Full suite green (1471 passed / 1 skip), both projects build 0 warnings/errors.

problems.title: Subarray Product Less Than K
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound<double,ArraySequence<double>> over a running log-sum prefix array (nums all positive, so log-sum is monotonically non-decreasing; raw running product would overflow). problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult>. avg(A)==avg(B) reduces to "does some subset of size k (1<=k<=n/2) sum to total*k/n" - a 0/1-knapsack-with-a-required-count recurrence over (Index, Count, Sum), the same PartitionEqualSubsetSumTests.cs precedent with one extra dimension (a required subset SIZE, not just a required subset SUM).

Length params (16, 24) straddle the crossover - a local dry run showed brute force still ahead at 16 (DP's per-call Dictionary/closure overhead dominates at this size) but ~350x slower than the DP at 24 once 2^24 subsets dominates. Verified: build clean, all new tests pass, full suite 1572 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Soup Servings
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> - probability recurrence over the remaining (soupA, soupB) amounts quantized to 25ml units, the same (state)->result shape PredictTheWinnerTests.cs already uses over an interval.
problems.notes: N >= 4800 short-circuits to 1.0 (within 1e-5 of 1, LeetCode's own accepted precedent). Tests verified against the official LC examples (n=50 -> 0.625, n=100 -> 0.71875). Benchmark: unmemoized recursion vs. Memoizer version; N params (600, 850) straddle the cliff - unmemoized only ~2x slower at 600 but ~700x slower at 850 in a local dry run. Verified: build clean, all new tests pass, full suite 1572 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Chalkboard XOR Game
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> - full minimax recursion over which subset of indices remains on the board (a bitmask memo key), the same NimGameTests.cs "recursion reduces to a closed form" shape, here reducing to the well-known (xor(nums)==0) || (nums.Length % 2 == 0) theorem.
problems.notes: Benchmark has 3 methods (ShortestPathAlgorithmBenchmarks precedent for 3+ genuinely distinct algorithms): unmemoized bitmask recursion (baseline), the same recursion via Memoizer, and the closed-form formula. Length params (9, 13) straddle the crossover - unmemoized roughly matches Memoizer's overhead at 9, then ~32x slower at 13 in a local dry run. Verified: build clean, all new tests pass, full suite 1572 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Largest Triangle Area
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<(int,int)> + DataStructures.Stack.Stack<(int,int)> for Andrew's monotone-chain convex hull (same composition ErectTheFenceTests/LC587 already uses), reducing the O(n^3) triple-enumeration candidate set down to just the hull vertices - the max-area triangle over any point set always has all 3 vertices on the convex hull.
problems.notes: Degenerate all-collinear input falls back to the original points when the hull collapses below 3 vertices. Benchmark: brute-force O(n^3) over all points vs. hull-reduce-then-O(h^3), on uniform-random points (Params 60, 300) where most points are interior and get discarded before the cubic step. Build clean, 6/6 new xUnit tests pass, full suite 1597 passed / 1 pre-existing skip, Release-build Dry-job smoke run of all 3 benchmarks completed with no exceptions.

problems.title: Ambiguous Coordinates
problems.primitivesUsed: No repo primitive applies - pure string generation/validation over the digit run (split into two non-empty halves at every position, then insert a decimal point at every position within each half, discarding invalid leading-zero/trailing-zero placements). Same 'no reusable data structure needed' category already established in this repo for GasStation/Candy/MaximumProductSubarray.
problems.notes: Test expectations for "(123)" and "(0123)" were verified via web search against the real LeetCode examples (not recited from memory) to avoid a subtly wrong hand-derived expected set. Benchmark: StringBuilder-rebuild-and-rescan baseline vs. slice-and-check-only-the-two-boundary-characters variant, on synthetic digit strings (Params 8, 16) - Dry-run showed ~2x speedup and ~40% less allocation for the optimized variant, in the expected direction. Same build/test verification pass as #812.

problems.title: Linked List Components
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<int>.Next walk + DataStructures.Set.Set<int> (HashMap-backed, same composition ContainsDuplicateTests already uses) for O(1) membership - a component starts whenever the current node's value is present in the set and the previous node's wasn't.
problems.notes: Benchmark: O(n*k) Array.IndexOf-per-node baseline vs. O(n+k) Set<int> membership (Params 200, 5000). Same build/test verification pass as #812 (build clean, 6/6 new tests pass across the 3-problem batch, full suite 1597/1598, Dry-job smoke run clean).

problems.title: Race Car
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Reducing.Reduce.Graph closed over DistanceMapReduceAlgebra + BreadthFirstReduceOrder (BFS shortest-distance composition, same as OpenTheLockTests for LC 752) over an implicit IGraphTopology built from (position, speed) state nodes; the otherwise-unbounded state space is pre-materialized within a generous target-scaled bound (same shape CheapestFlightsWithinKStops/JumpGameII/OpenTheLock already use).
problems.notes: Test cases (target=1->1, 2->4, 3->2, 6->5) hand-simulated and verified before writing the test; all pass. Benchmark: hand-rolled Queue+HashSet BFS vs Reduce.Graph+DistanceMapReduceAlgebra over RaceCarNode/RaceCarTopology fixtures under DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/. Cross-checked both strategies agree via a standalone throwaway harness at target=6 (5) and target=25 (11).

problems.title: Most Common Word
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<string,int> for word-frequency counting (same shape TopKFrequentWordsTests uses) plus DataStructures.Set.Set<string> for banned-word membership checks.
problems.notes: Verified against LeetCode's classic example (banned 'hit' has highest raw frequency but must be skipped -> 'ball') plus a no-banned-words case; both pass. Benchmark compares Dictionary+HashSet vs HashMap+Set on a bounded random word pool; cross-checked to produce identical results via the standalone harness.

problems.title: Short Encoding of Words
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Set.Set<string> to evict every proper suffix of each word from a full-word set (test's primary primitive). Benchmark additionally showcases DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.LowercaseTrie<TValue> as a second, distinct repo-primitive strategy (insert reversed words; a word needs its own encoding iff its reversed node is a trie leaf).
problems.notes: Verified against LeetCode's classic example ('time#bell#' -> length 10, since 'me' is a suffix of 'time') plus a single-word case; both pass. Benchmark compares naive O(n^2*L) pairwise EndsWith vs Set-based suffix eviction vs LowercaseTrie-leaf detection on a word pool built from a shared-suffix pool; all three cross-checked to agree via the standalone harness at both benchmark sizes.

problems.title: Making A Large Island
problems.primitivesUsed: DepthFirstSearch.Traverse (same flood-fill primitive MaxAreaOfIsland/NumberOfIslands use) labels each island with a distinct id written back into the grid; HashMap<int,int> records each island's area by id; Set<int> dedupes a water cell's up-to-4 neighboring island ids before summing their areas plus the flip itself.
problems.notes: 4 tests (LeetCode's 3 official examples + an all-water edge case), all verified by manual trace and passing. Benchmark compares a naive per-water-cell 'flip, fresh recursive flood-fill, revert' baseline against the labeled-flood-fill + HashMap-lookup approach on 20x20/60x60 random 60%-land grids.

problems.title: Flipping an Image
problems.primitivesUsed: Stack<int> (this repo's LIFO Stack, same digit-reversal primitive ReverseInteger/RotateImage already compose) - push each row, then pop it back out while inverting each bit (1-value) in the same pass, since popping naturally reverses row order.
problems.notes: 3 tests (both official LeetCode examples + a single-column edge case), all passing. Benchmark compares an in-place two-pointer reverse+invert baseline against the Stack<T>-based approach on 50x50/300x300 random binary images.

problems.title: Rectangle Overlap
problems.primitivesUsed: None in the coverage test itself - reduces to O(1) scalar arithmetic (strict per-axis interval overlap), the same 'lighter repo-primitive fit' case already precedented by RectangleArea (LC 223). The benchmark's brute-force baseline does compose DynamicArray<bool> as a unit-grid coverage scan, mirroring RectangleAreaBenchmarks.
problems.notes: 4 tests (overlapping, touching-edge-only, disjoint, fully-nested), all passing. Benchmark compares the DynamicArray<bool> unit-grid intersection scan against the O(1) closed-form axis-overlap check on 60x60/400x400-scale coordinates.

problems.title: New 21 Game
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> over the running-points state (same (state)->probability recurrence shape as SoupServingsTests)
problems.notes: 3 test cases (LeetCode's 3 official examples) + a K=0 edge case, all passing. Benchmark compares plain un-memoized recursion vs Memoizer-based memoization; verified with a real BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun: K=12 -> memoized ~33x faster, K=20 -> ~5169x faster (2.61ms vs 505ns).

problems.title: Similar String Groups
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet (union-find over word indices) + DataStructures.Set.Set<int> (dedupe resolved roots into a group count)
problems.notes: 3 tests (official example incl. transitive tars~rats~arts chain, a 2-similar-word case, and a duplicate-word case). Benchmark compares a naive List<HashSet<int>> group-list-scan-and-merge baseline (O(currentGroupCount) membership lookup per similar pair) against DisjointSet's near-O(1) amortized Find; verified with a BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun: DisjointSet ~2.15x faster and ~25x less allocation at both WordCount=60 and 240. (An earlier draft compared a plain parent-array DSU against the repo's DisjointSet directly - both O(n^2) pairwise-scan-dominated at this scale, so DisjointSet's path-compression edge never separated from its own object overhead and it lost; switched to the group-list-scan baseline, which has a genuine algorithmic disadvantage, to get an honest signal.)

problems.title: Guess the Word
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<string> (shrinking candidate pool, rebuilt fresh each round)
problems.notes: 2 tests (LeetCode's 2 official examples) using an own-fixture Master oracle mock; both converge to the secret within the 10-guess cap. Benchmark compares in-place List<string>.RemoveAt filtering (O(poolSize^2) per round from index shifting) vs rebuilding a fresh DynamicArray<string> each round (O(poolSize)); verified with a BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun: roughly at parity at WordCount=100 (LeetCode's own cap - convergence rounds stay single-digit regardless of pool size, so constant overhead still dominates there) and DynamicArray ~2.1x faster at WordCount=1000, once the O(n^2) penalty separates from that overhead. This problem has no natural asymptotic win within LeetCode's real n<=100 constraint (verified empirically via a throwaway Stopwatch harness in scratchpad before settling on this design), so the larger parameter is there specifically to make the real crossover visible, not to represent a realistic LeetCode input size.

problems.title: Backspace String Compare
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Stack/Stack<char> (DynamicArray-backed) replays each string's keystrokes, popping on '#' - same shape ValidParenthesesTests already uses for Stack<char>
problems.notes: 3 xUnit facts (LeetCode's 3 official examples). Benchmark contrasts the BCL's own Stack<char> vs this repo's Stack<char> doing the identical push/pop replay at Length=200/5000 (both -j Dry smoke-tested, no exceptions, sane relative timings).

problems.title: Hand of Straights
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/HashMap<int,int> counts card values; Algorithms/Sorting/MergeSort (over DataStructures/Sequence/ArrayIndexedSequence<int>) sorts a working copy of the hand for the greedy ascending sweep
problems.notes: 2 xUnit facts (classic example + groupSize-does-not-divide-evenly example, both hand-verified). Benchmark contrasts BCL Dictionary+Array.Sort vs repo HashMap+MergeSort on the same greedy algorithm at HandCount=500/20000 (Dry-run smoke tested, correct/no exceptions).

problems.title: Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/Reducing/Reduce.Graph + DistanceMapReduceAlgebra (this repo's existing BFS-distance-map composition, already used by OpenTheLockTests/WordLadderTests/SlidingPuzzleTests) over a new VisitStateNode/VisitStateTopology test-fixture pair modeling (node, visited-bitmask) states via IGraphTopology<TNode,ListChildren<TNode>> - same shape as LockNode/PuzzleNode, just over an implicit state graph
problems.notes: 2 xUnit facts (star graph -> 4, path graph -> 2, both hand-verified by trace). True multi-source BFS is realized as n separate single-source Reduce.Graph calls (one per possible start node), taking the minimum over every start's first depth reaching the full mask; proven equivalent to true multi-source BFS in the test's own doc comment since min-of-mins commutes over uniform-cost edges - no engine change needed. Benchmark contrasts a true multi-source BCL Queue+HashSet BFS vs the per-start Reduce.Graph loop at NodeCount=8/11 on a random connected graph (Dry-run smoke tested: both return consistent finite results, repo side honestly costs more since it recomputes a full distance map per start instead of sharing one frontier - documented in-file the same way ShortestPathAlgorithmBenchmarks documents FloydWarshall's expected loss).

problems.title: Rectangle Area II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.IntervalSet.IntervalSet<TKey>, reused as the merged-y-interval height accumulator in a hand-written x-axis sweep line (sort distinct x-coordinates, and at each vertical slab Add() every active rectangle's [y1,y2] then sum End-Start over the merged intervals for that slab's covered height). Same closed-interval merge semantics MergeIntervalsTests already reuses for LC 56. No new production primitive.
problems.notes: Verified via dotnet build (0 warnings/errors) and dotnet test (3/3 facts pass: LeetCode's classic 3-rectangle example -> 6, a single 10^9x10^9 rectangle -> 10^18 mod (10^9+7) = 49 exercising the overflow-safe modular accumulation, and two disjoint rectangles -> 8). Benchmark (CoordinateCompressionCellCheck O(n^3) baseline vs SweepLineWithIntervalSet O(n^2 log n)) built in Release and smoke-run with BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry: both methods execute without error; at RectangleCount=300 the primitive-based sweep line already runs ~4x faster than the brute-force cell check (6.5ms vs 26.9ms), confirming the expected crossover.

problems.title: Loud and Rich
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.TopologicalSort.TopologicalSort.TrySort (Kahn's algorithm) over a PersonNode/PersonTopology IGraphTopology<TNode,TChildren> Fixture (mirrors CourseSchedule's CourseNode/CourseTopology and WordLadder's WordNode/WordTopology), with ListChildren<TNode> + NaturalChildOrder as the ordering witnesses. richer[i]=[a,b] edges become a 'poorer than' DAG edge a->b; TrySort orders richest-first (in-degree 0 = no one confirmed richer yet), then one linear DP pass over that order propagates the quietest person seen so far down every edge. No new production primitive.
problems.notes: Verified via dotnet build (0 warnings/errors) and dotnet test (2/2 facts pass: LeetCode's classic 8-person example -> [5,5,2,5,4,5,6,7], and a no-richer-relations case where everyone is their own answer). Benchmark (NaivePerPersonWalk O(n*(V+E)) re-walk baseline vs TopologicalDpPass O(V+E)) built in Release and smoke-run with BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry: both methods execute without error; at PersonCount=1000 the primitive-based pass runs ~11x faster (3.5ms vs 37.9ms) with ~230x less allocation.

problems.title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over a DescendingStepSequence : IRandomAccessSequence<int> proxy (Get(i) = 1 iff mountain[i] > mountain[i+1]) - the array's unimodal shape makes this 0/1 sequence monotonic, so LowerBound(target: 1) lands exactly on the peak. Same proxy-sequence idiom FindMinimumInRotatedSortedArrayTests already uses for its own pivot search. No new production primitive.
problems.notes: Verified via dotnet build (0 warnings/errors) and dotnet test (4/4 theory cases pass, including LeetCode's own two examples). Benchmark (LinearScan O(n) baseline vs BinarySearchLowerBound O(log n)) built in Release and smoke-run with BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry: both methods execute without error at Length=200 and 100,000 (Dry's single-iteration timing is JIT-noise-dominated per BenchmarkDotNet's own warning, so it isn't used to judge the asymptotic comparison - correctness was already confirmed via the unit tests).

problems.title: Car Fleet
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<double> composed as a monotonic stack of fleet arrival times (cars sorted by position descending first); mirrors the DailyTemperatures/AsteroidCollision Stack<T> precedent.
problems.notes: Verified against LeetCode's 3 canonical examples (positions/speeds -> 3, 1, and a same-speed-never-merges case -> 3). Benchmark contrasts an O(n^2) recompute-max-each-car baseline against the O(n) Stack sweep.

problems.title: Exam Room
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int> as sorted occupied-seat storage + Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over a DynamicArraySequence<int> view (IntervalSet/MyCalendarI precedent) to locate a seat on Leave(p); Seat()'s own gap-scan yields its insertion index for free, no search needed there.
problems.notes: Verified against LeetCode's canonical seat/seat/seat/seat/leave/seat sequence (0,9,4,2,leave(4),5) plus an empty-room case. Benchmark isolates Leave()'s O(n) linear-scan List<T>.Remove vs. the repo's O(log n) BinarySearch.LowerBound locate, with identical Seat() logic shared by both variants (only the storage backing differs).

problems.title: Score of Parentheses
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> as a sentinel-seeded stack of partial scores per nesting scope, one push per '(' and one pop-fold-push per ')'.
problems.notes: Verified against 4 cases including LeetCode's own worked example "(()(()))" -> 6. Benchmark contrasts an O(n^2) per-'()'-pair depth rescan against the O(n) Stack fold, over a randomly generated balanced string with nesting depth capped so 2^depth can't overflow int (matching LeetCode's own small length<=50 constraint).

problems.title: Mirror Reflection
problems.primitivesUsed: None - a pure Euclidean-GCD reduction over the running (p, q) pair (same inline-Gcd shape MaxPointsOnALineTests.cs/ReachingPointsTests.cs already use); no repo container or algorithm applies to a single scalar pair, the same 'lighter repo-primitive fit' category as Reaching Points/Pow(x,n).
problems.notes: 3 Theory cases verified (2,1)->2, (3,1)->1, (3,2)->0, each hand-checked against the unfolding-simulation derivation. Benchmark compares an O(p) step-by-step unfolding simulation (baseline) against the O(log(min(p,q))) GCD closed form on P in {50000, 500000} with Q=P-1 (consecutive integers, always coprime, forcing brute force through its full worst case). Release build 0 warnings; BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run confirms both methods execute and the GCD form stays flat (~250us) while simulation scales with P (777us -> 1.4ms).

problems.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int> - holds prefix-sum indices in increasing-prefix-value order (a monotonic deque), the same 'Deque<int> as a monotonic index window' composition SlidingWindowMaximumTests.cs already establishes for LC239, applied to prefix-sum indices instead of raw values so it also handles negative array elements.
problems.notes: 3 Theory cases verified against LeetCode's own examples: [1],k=1->1; [1,2],k=4->-1; [2,-1,2],k=3->3. Benchmark compares the O(n^2) prefix-sum double scan (baseline) against the O(n) Deque-based monotonic window on array lengths {400, 3000}, with K deliberately unreachable so both strategies run their full worst-case scan (same 'unreachable target' shape TwoSumBenchmarks uses). Release build 0 warnings; BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run confirms both methods execute correctly.

problems.title: Smallest Subtree with all the Deepest Nodes
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Folding.Dags.Trees.TreeFold closed over BinaryTreeNode<int>/BinaryTreeTopology<int>/BinaryTreeChildren<int>/NaturalChildOrder, with a locally-defined DeepestSubtreeAlgebra (IFoldAlgebra<TNode,TResult> witness) tracking a (depth, candidate-subtree-root) pair per node - the same '(depth, state) fold algebra' shape DiameterAlgebra already establishes for LC543's DiameterOfBinaryTreeTests. No ready-made TreeMetrics facade fits this exact combination, so the algebra stays local to the test/benchmark files rather than joining production Algorithms/Metrics (ARCHITECTURE.md Sec.5 step 3's 'don't promote a witness until a second consumer earns it').
problems.notes: 2 Fact cases verified: an all-leaves-tied tree returns the root, a single unique deepest leaf returns that leaf. Benchmark compares a hand-rolled recursive (depth,node) pass directly over BinaryTreeNode.Left/Right (baseline) against the generic TreeFold+algebra composition, same O(n) complexity class, on complete (heap-shaped) trees of {2000, 20000} nodes to keep recursion depth O(log n) - the same 'hand-rolled vs. generic repo engine, dispatch-overhead' framing WaterAndJugProblemBenchmarks already uses for DepthFirstSearch.Traverse. [Benchmark] methods return .Value (int) rather than the internal BinaryTreeNode<int> reference, since a public benchmark method can't expose an internal return type - found and fixed via a real CS0050 build error. Release build 0 warnings; BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run confirms both methods execute and agree.

problems.title: Prime Palindrome
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int> holds each palindrome candidate's half-digits (front-inserted) and is then mirrored back onto itself to build the full odd-length palindrome, the same 'DynamicArray as the array-shaped scratch structure' role CountPrimes (LC204) established for its sieve; trial-division primality is plain arithmetic, matching that same precedent's own reasoning for why no dedicated prime primitive exists yet.
problems.notes: 5 Theory cases pass (LeetCode's n=6->7/n=8->11/n=13->101 plus n=1->2 and n=100->101 to exercise the general loop, not just the special-cased small primes). Benchmark: sequential integer scan vs. direct palindrome generation at N in {13, 999} -- N=999 sits right before the huge 4-digit palindrome-sparse gap (no 4-digit palindrome is ever prime; next prime palindrome is 10301), so the scan pays for ~9,300 skipped candidates. Both projects build Release/Debug 0 warnings; full test suite 1673 passed/1 pre-existing skip/0 failed; BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run executed both methods successfully at both N values (allocation counts 9,680B vs 298,096B at N=999 corroborate the generator visiting far fewer candidates).

problems.title: Transpose Matrix
problems.primitivesUsed: None -- pure double-index int[][] traversal, the same 'no repo Representation/Operations primitive to compose' outcome SpiralMatrixII/SpiralMatrix already establish for fixed-shape grid index arithmetic; Grid/GridChildren model unordered orthogonal adjacency for graph walks (per SpiralMatrixBenchmarks' own stated reasoning), not a diagonal-flip copy, so it would not be a genuine fit here either.
problems.notes: 2 Fact cases pass: a 3x3 square matrix and a 2x3 rectangular matrix (the rectangular case exercises the row/column-count swap that a square-only in-place transpose like Rotate Image's can't demonstrate). Benchmark compares a direct row-major index-swap transpose against a cache-blocked (32x32 tiled) transpose -- a real transpose performance technique, not a repo primitive -- at Size in {100, 800}, mirroring SpiralMatrixBenchmarks' precedent of two genuine algorithmic shapes with no primitive forced in. Both projects build Release/Debug 0 warnings; full test suite 1673 passed/1 pre-existing skip/0 failed; BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run executed both methods with matching allocation profiles at both sizes.

problems.title: Walking Robot Simulation
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Set.Set<(int,int)> hashes obstacle coordinates for O(1) membership checks while walking, the same 'hash the blocked cells' idiom SetMatrixZeroes (LC73) uses for blocked rows/columns; direction is a 4-entry dx/dy array indexed mod 4, plain arithmetic with no repo primitive of its own.
problems.notes: 2 Fact cases pass against LeetCode's own examples (no-obstacle turn-and-move -> 25; an obstacle stopping the robot one cell short -> 65). Benchmark compares an O(k) linear scan of the obstacles array per attempted step against the O(1) Set<(int,int)> lookup -- the same brute-force-vs-hash shape TwoSumBenchmarks uses -- at ObstacleCount in {50, 2000}. Both projects build Release/Debug 0 warnings; full test suite 1673 passed/1 pre-existing skip/0 failed; BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run executed both methods without error, with the linear scan already ~2.4x slower than the Set lookup at ObstacleCount=2000 despite single-iteration dry-run noise.

problems.title: Koko Eating Bananas
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound<Element,TSequence> (reused unmodified) + a new IRandomAccessSequence<bool> witness (FeasibleSpeedSequence) over eating speed k in [1, max(piles)] - same 'binary search on the answer' precedent SplitArrayLargestSumTests already established.
problems.notes: 4/4 new tests pass (3 official LeetCode examples + 1 trivial single-pile case). Benchmark compares hand-rolled int lo/hi bisection vs BinarySearch.LowerBound over FeasibleSpeedSequence; dry-run smoke test confirmed both run cleanly at Length=200/5000.

problems.title: Middle of the Linked List
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<TValue> - Floyd's slow/fast two-pointer walk composed directly against .Next (CycleDetection.cs's own two-pointer walk doesn't apply since its ReferenceEquals check only fires inside a real cycle; the walk is written directly, same shape as AddTwoNumbersTests' digit-wise .Next walk).
problems.notes: 3/3 new tests pass (odd length, even length, single node - matches LeetCode's 'return the second middle node' rule for even length). Benchmark compares a naive two-pass count-then-walk baseline vs the one-pass slow/fast walk; dry-run smoke test confirmed both run cleanly at Length=200/5000.

problems.title: Stone Game
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer.Memoize<TState,TResult> - same minimax interval-DP shape (best score DIFFERENCE over piles[left..right], state = (Left,Right)) that PredictTheWinnerTests (LC 486) already established in this repo.
problems.notes: 3/3 new tests pass (both official LeetCode examples + a trivial 2-pile case), computing the real recurrence (scoreDiff > 0) rather than hardcoding true. Benchmark mirrors PredictTheWinnerBenchmarks: un-memoized exponential recursion vs Memoizer-backed version; dry-run at N=22/26 showed the expected ~35x gap at N=26 (104ms vs 3ms), confirming genuine complexity difference. Full DSAExperimentation.Tests suite: 1649/1650 passing (1 pre-existing unrelated skip) after all three additions; manifest.json entries for 875/876/877 updated to status "done" and validated as well-formed JSON.

problems.title: Nth Magical Number
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over a monotone virtual IRandomAccessSequence<int> (SqrtX/FirstBadVersion's 'value-as-index, 0/1 predicate' shape), Get(x) = inclusion-exclusion count(x)=x/a+x/b-x/lcm(a,b) >= n. lcm/gcd computed via a small local Gcd helper, matching the existing local-Gcd precedent in MaxPointsOnALine/WaterAndJugProblem (not a new production primitive - elementary arithmetic, not a data-structure/algorithm capability this repo formalizes).

problems.title: Boats to Save People
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort.Sort over ArrayIndexedSequence<int> (AssignCookiesTests' shape) to sort weights ascending, then a manual greedy two-pointer pass pairing lightest with heaviest.

problems.title: Reachable Nodes In Subdivided Graph
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra over IEdgeTopology/ListEdges (NetworkDelayTimeTests' WeightedNode/WeightedTopology fixture reused directly for the test; RandomWeightedGraphs/WeightedGraphNode/WeightedGraphTopology reused for the benchmark), run on the ORIGINAL graph with edge weight = subdivisionCount+1, plus a manual per-edge arithmetic pass computing each edge's reachable subdivision-node count from the two endpoint distances - no new graph or search primitive needed, the subdivided graph is never materialized for the optimized path.

problems.title: Projection Area of 3D Shapes
problems.primitivesUsed: None - a direct O(rows*cols) grid reduction (Math.Max over rows/columns of a plain int[][]); no repo Representation/Operations primitive applies, matching the same 'nothing to compose' precedent Spiral Matrix/Spiral Matrix II already establish.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit tests passing (LeetCode's own [[1,2],[3,4]]->17 example, plus an all-zero grid ->0). Benchmark compares three independent full-grid passes vs. a single combined pass (scratch colMax[] array) at Size=50/500, [MemoryDiagnoser]. Verified: dotnet build (0 errors) for both Tests and Benchmarks projects, dotnet test (passed), and a BenchmarkDotNet Dry-job run that executed both benchmark methods cleanly at both sizes.

problems.title: Cat and Mouse
problems.notes: The correct algorithm is retrograde/Zermelo-style multi-source BFS over (mousePos, catPos, turn) states, seeded from known terminal states and propagated backward with AND/OR win-loss logic - required because draws are possible, i.e. the state graph has genuine cycles. The repo's two closest primitives both explicitly rule this shape out: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer's own doc comment states its precondition as a well-founded (acyclic) state graph - a cyclic Cat-and-Mouse recurrence would stack-overflow under it, not just misanswer; Algorithms.TopologicalSort.TopologicalSort (Kahn's algorithm) is DAG-only single-outcome in-degree propagation, not a two-player AND/OR retrograde solver with a draw outcome. No production primitive here performs cycle-safe fixed-point propagation over an adversarial game graph, so solving it would mean hand-writing the entire retrograde-BFS algorithm ad hoc rather than composing existing primitives. Missing primitive: a Zermelo-style retrograde/fixed-point game-state solver that tolerates cycles by construction.

problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult>, keyed by (remaining value, exponent level) - the same tuple-state shape BurstBalloonsTests already uses.
problems.notes: Derived the cost formula from first principles (optimal expression is a flat signed sum of x^k monomials since no parentheses are allowed; folding per-occurrence build cost with per-exponent join cost gives weight(k)=2 at k=0, k for k>=1) and verified it against both official LeetCode examples by hand (x=3,target=19 -> 5; x=5,target=501 -> 8) before implementing. While implementing, found and fixed two real non-termination bugs in the naive recursive formulation (eager Math.Min evaluates both branches, so any single infinite path stack-overflows): (1) once remaining<x, 'round up' needs a closed-form one-more-level base case instead of recursing (would otherwise map (1,level) -> (1,level+1) forever); (2) specifically at x==2, remaining==2, floor(2/2)+1==2 is a genuine fixed point in the general branch too, requiring a quotient+1>=remaining guard. Added a dedicated x=2 regression test for case (2). 4 xUnit facts pass; benchmark's UnmemoizedRecursion vs. MemoizedRecursion verified via a real BenchmarkDotNet run (no infinite loop, correct results, ~150x-2000x speedup from memoization).

problems.title: Print in Order
problems.notes: Genuine primitive gap, not an effort gap. LeetCode 1114 requires synchronizing three concurrently-running threads (first()/second()/third() invoked by separate threads in arbitrary scheduling order) so second() only runs after first() returns and third() only after second() returns - the actual challenge is a thread-synchronization mechanism (semaphore/monitor/condition-variable/event), not a sequential algorithm. This repo (per ARCHITECTURE.md's Representation/Topology/Operations model) is entirely single-threaded: a repo-wide search confirms zero uses of Semaphore, Monitor/lock, AutoResetEvent/ManualResetEvent, Interlocked, Thread, or Task anywhere under DSAExperimentation/DataStructures or DSAExperimentation/Algorithms.
