problems.title: Find Winner on a Tic Tac Toe Game
problems.primitivesUsed: None beyond plain fixed-size row/column/diagonal running-count arrays - same 'no stronger reusable repo primitive beyond ordinary array bookkeeping' shape JumpGameTests already documents; this problem is O(1) extra space by nature, and Grid/GridNode model pathfinding adjacency, not score tracking, so they would not be a genuine fit.
problems.notes: Benchmark generalizes to an n x n board (LC1275 fixes n=3) to give BenchmarkDotNet a [Params] axis: rebuild-and-rescan-every-move (O(moves*lines*size)) vs. the incremental running-count check the test uses (O(moves)) - same 'two genuinely different algorithms, no data structure' shape SpiralMatrixBenchmarks/RotateImageBenchmarks already set. Dry-run showed the gap widening from ~2x at Size=10 to ~12.5x at Size=60. 4/4 tests pass, verified via the same isolated-project workaround noted above.

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning III
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer over state (Position, PartitionsLeft) driving the partition-count recurrence; a plain local two-pointer helper (same shape as PalindromePartitioningTests' IsPalindrome, generalized to count mismatches) prices each candidate substring's repair cost - no new production primitive needed.
problems.notes: 3/3 theory cases pass ("abc",2->1; "aabbc",3->0; "leetcode",8->0). Benchmark: NaiveRecursion (unmemoized double recursion) vs MemoizedTopDown (Memoizer), string length 12/18 with k=length/2.

problems.title: Iterator for Combination
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.Search (CombinationSumIII/PalindromePartitioning precedent) enumerates increasing-index combinations, which is already lexicographic order since the input is sorted; CombinationIterator itself is just a List<string> + cursor over that precomputed, already-ordered result (same 'no algorithm primitive beyond a cursor' shape as BinarySearchTreeIteratorTests).
problems.notes: 2/2 tests pass (classic "abc"/2 example yielding ab,ac,bc in order; combinationLength==characterCount edge case). Benchmark: BitmaskEnumeration (brute-force 2^n subset scan + sort) vs BacktrackComposed (Backtrack.Search), characters length 10/16 with combinationLength=length/2.

problems.title: Convert Binary Number in a Linked List to Integer
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<TValue>.Next walked directly, accumulating value=(value<<1)|bit - no algorithm primitive needed beyond the node representation itself, same shape as MiddleOfTheLinkedListTests' walk.
problems.notes: 3/3 tests pass ([1,0,1]->5; [0]->0; all-ones->31). Benchmark: CollectThenFold (two-pass, buffers bits then folds positional weights) vs SinglePassShift (value = (value<<1)|bit in one walk), list length 200/5000.

problems.title: All Elements in Two Binary Search Trees
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.InOrderTraversal/IInOrderHooks over BinaryTreeNode<int> (plus BinarySearchTree<int> to build fixtures in the benchmark) collecting into DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int>; the two ascending in-order sequences are then combined with a plain two-pointer merge (no sort needed).

problems.title: Jump Game III
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse<TNode> closed over a bare Func<int,IEnumerable<int>> successor relation (i -> i+arr[i], i-arr[i], bounds-filtered) — reachability over an implicit bidirectional-hop graph, no new primitive needed.

problems.title: Distinct Echo Substrings
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.RollingHash.RollingHash (O(1) equality screen per (start,halfLength) pair, verified with a real SequenceEqual — the same screen-then-verify shape RollingHashSearch/LongestChunkedPalindromeDecomposition already use) plus DataStructures.Set.Set<string> (HashMap-backed) to dedupe found echo substrings by text.

problems.title: Number of Operations to Make Network Connected
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet (union-find, path compression + union-by-rank) to count connected components, plus DataStructures.Set.Set<int> to dedupe roots - the exact same composition NumberOfProvincesTests already uses; answer is componentCount-1, or -1 when connections.Length < n-1

problems.title: Print Words Vertically
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<char> as the growable per-column char buffer (StreamOfCharactersTests precedent), trailing spaces trimmed in place via RemoveAt(Count-1) instead of a separate TrimEnd pass over a materialized string

problems.title: Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors at a Threshold Distance
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.AllPairsShortestPaths (Floyd-Warshall) over the existing WeightedNode/WeightedTopology IEdgeTopology fixtures (roads wired both directions since LC1334's roads are undirected) - the same primitive AllPairsShortestPathsTests already exercises, here answering an all-pairs reachability-count question instead of a single-pair lookup; benchmark contrasts it against n separate ShortestPath.Dijkstra calls

problems.title: Jump Game V
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.TopologicalSort.TopologicalSort.TrySort (Kahn's algorithm) over an implicit graph where edge i->j exists only when arr[i] strictly exceeds every value strictly between i and j and arr[j] itself, guaranteeing a DAG; the returned topological order then drives one linear longest-path relaxation pass (plain Dictionary, glue logic in the test/benchmark, not a new production primitive).
problems.notes: 3/3 new tests pass (2 official LC examples + 1 edge case), all cross-checked against a standalone Python memoized-recursion reference before hardcoding expected values. Full suite: 2021 passed / 1 pre-existing unrelated skip / 0 failed. Benchmark: per-start memoized DFS baseline vs TopologicalSort.TrySort+relaxation; dry run confirmed correctness on both sides, primitive side ~8.5x slower / ~5x more allocation due to Kahn's bookkeeping overhead - included as proof of sufficiency, not speed, mirroring JumpGameIIBenchmarks' own precedent.

problems.title: Jump Game IV
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra over an implicit unit-weight hop graph (i->i+1, i-1, and every same-value index), reusing Tests/Algorithms/ShortestPaths/Fixtures' WeightedNode/WeightedTopology/ListEdges - the exact composition JumpGameIITests already established for the sibling problem (LC 45).
problems.notes: 4/4 new tests pass (3 official LC examples + 1 single-element edge case), cross-checked against a standalone Python BFS reference. Full suite: 2021 passed / 1 pre-existing unrelated skip / 0 failed. Benchmark: hand-rolled BFS with the standard 'clear value-group after first use' trick vs Dijkstra over the explicit hop graph; dry run confirmed correctness, primitive side ~6-8x slower (priority-queue overhead on what's really unweighted BFS).

problems.title: Tweet Counts Per Frequency
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<string,DynamicArray<int>> composed with DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int> - per-tweet-name bucket of recorded times, the same per-key-bucket shape DesignTwitterTests' _tweetsByUser already uses; query buckets each in-range time via straight division by the requested frequency's chunk size.
problems.notes: 2/2 new tests pass (official LC example + a no-recorded-tweets edge case). Full suite: 2021 passed / 1 pre-existing unrelated skip / 0 failed. Benchmark: flat list scanned+filtered by name per query vs per-name HashMap<string,DynamicArray<int>> grouping done once at record time; dry run confirmed correctness and the expected win (~0.69x-0.40x of baseline, i.e. up to ~2.5x faster, growing with TweetCount).

problems.title: Maximum Students Taking Exam
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer keyed on a (Row,PrevMask) tuple - same 2D-tuple memo-state shape LongestIncreasingPathInAMatrixTests/SmallestSufficientTeamTests already establish, combined into one key. Row masks validated against broken seats + self-adjacency; row-to-row transitions validated against the previous row's mask shifted one bit each way for the diagonal-cheating check.
problems.notes: 4/4 new tests pass (3 official LC examples + all-broken-seats edge case). Build clean, filtered test run green. Benchmark: unmemoized bitmask recursion vs. Memoizer-routed recursion over an all-open RowCount x 6 grid; BenchmarkDotNet Dry-run confirmed both execute and agree, with a ~2.4x win for memoization at RowCount=5. At RowCount=3 memoization briefly loses to constant overhead - confirmed this is not specific to this benchmark by reproducing the identical crossover on the already-committed CanIWinBenchmarks at its own smallest Dry-run param.

problems.title: Product of the Last K Numbers
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<long> as a running prefix-product array - TimeBasedKeyValueStoreTests' 'parallel/running DynamicArray history' shape. Add(0) resets to a fresh [1] prefix instead of dividing by zero; GetProduct(k) is one division of two prefix entries.
problems.notes: 3/3 new tests pass (official LC example sequence + no-zeros edge case + k=1-right-after-a-zero edge case). Build clean, filtered test run green. Benchmark: O(k) raw-stream replay vs. O(1) prefix-product division, structure pre-built in GlobalSetup; BenchmarkDotNet Dry-run confirmed both execute and agree bit-for-bit (both overflow long identically at stress sizes, harmless for throughput-only measurement).

problems.title: Apply Discount Every n Orders
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,int> mapping product id to price - TwoSumTests' 'one HashMap, O(1) lookup per line item' shape, built once in the constructor. GetBill sums looked-up-price * amount per line item and applies the discount whenever the running customer count is a multiple of n.
problems.notes: 2/2 new tests pass (official LC example sequence, discounted on 3rd/6th calls + n=1 every-call-discounted edge case). Build clean, filtered test run green. Benchmark: TwoSumBenchmarks' O(n) linear-scan vs O(1) HashMap contrast applied to Cashier's price lookup, catalog pre-built in GlobalSetup; BenchmarkDotNet Dry-run confirmed both execute, agree, and show the expected ~4.3x win at ProductCount=5000.

problems.title: Count All Valid Pickup and Delivery Options
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer over the recurrence f(i)=f(i-1)*i*(2i-1) mod 1e9+7 (same idiom as UniqueBinarySearchTreesTests/NumberOfMusicPlaylistsTests); benchmark compares iterative tabulation vs. Memoizer.

problems.title: Validate Binary Tree Nodes
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet (indegree check + union-find cycle/connectivity check), the same composition RedundantConnectionTests/RedundantConnectionIITests already use; benchmark contrasts an O(n^2) naive per-candidate-root traversal rescan against the single O(n*alpha(n)) DisjointSet pass.

problems.title: Closest Divisors
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over a monotone DataStructures.Sequence.IRandomAccessSequence virtual sequence to locate floor(sqrt(candidate)) (same technique as SqrtXTests), then a short walk down to the nearest exact divisor; benchmark contrasts full-range O(candidate) brute-force divisor scan vs. the sqrt-anchored walk.

problems.title: How Many Numbers Are Smaller Than the Current Number
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort (over ArrayIndexedSequence<int>) to sort a copy, then Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound (over ArraySequence<int>) per element - the leftmost insertion index LowerBound returns is exactly the count of strictly smaller elements.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares O(n^2) brute-force pairwise counting vs sort-once-then-LowerBound-per-element O(n log n). Dry run confirmed the crossover at Length=5000 (~4.9ms vs ~45ms).

problems.title: Linked List in Binary Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinaryTreeNode<TValue> + DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<TValue> - same 'try every node as a start, recurse into both children' shape SubtreeOfAnotherTreeTests already establishes, matching a linked-list chain via .Next instead of a second tree.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a naive array-slice-per-recursive-step baseline (int[1..] reallocated on every match check) vs walking the given SinglyLinkedListNode<TValue>.Next chain directly. Dry run confirmed zero allocation for the linked-node walk vs ~4MB for the array-slice walk at NodeCount=2000, plus a real speed gap.

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Make at Least One Valid Path in a Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<Element,TOrder> ordered by DataStructures.Graph.ShortestPaths.ByPriorityOrder<TNode,TWeight> - the same Dijkstra-shaped grid frontier SwimInRisingWaterTests already proves, here summing 0/1 edge costs (0 to follow a cell's own arrow, 1 to override it) with settle-once bookkeeping mirroring ShortestPath.cs's own Explore loop (additive costs need settle-at-pop, unlike SwimInRisingWater's minimax settle-at-push shortcut).
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a textbook O(V^2) linear-scan Dijkstra vs the repo's Heap-backed O(E log V) frontier, same comparison shape as ShortestPathAlgorithmBenchmarks/SwimInRisingWaterBenchmarks. Dry run showed the expected crossover by Size=40 (~5.1ms heap vs ~9.6ms naive).

problems.title: Maximum Sum BST in Binary Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: BinaryTreeNode<TValue> (DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees) via direct hand-rolled post-order recursion, not TreeFold/BinaryTreeChildren (which compact away missing-child positional identity that a BST check needs) - same shape as existing ValidateBinarySearchTreeTests/BinaryTreeMaximumPathSumTests precedent.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares O(n^2) per-node revalidate-and-resum vs the O(n) bottom-up single pass; verified with --job Dry (36.9ms vs 1.17ms at n=2000).

problems.title: Design a Stack With Increment Operation
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Stack/Stack<int> (two instances - one live, one scratch), same composition MinStackTests already uses.
problems.notes: Increment implemented via full drain-into-scratch-and-rebuild since Stack<T>'s public surface is deliberately LIFO-only (no indexer). Benchmark honestly shows this O(size)-per-call cost vs an array-backed O(k)-per-call baseline; verified with --job Dry.

problems.title: Balance a Binary Search Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: InOrderTraversal.Walk/IInOrderHooks + DynamicArray<int> to collect sorted values, then BinaryTreeNode<int> midpoint-split rebuild (same helper ConvertSortedArrayToBinarySearchTreeTests already uses).
problems.notes: Same composition FindModeInBinarySearchTreeTests/KthSmallestElementInABSTTests already establish for InOrderTraversal + DynamicArray. Benchmark compares O(n^2) repeated-kth-smallest-scan baseline vs the O(n) one-pass InOrderTraversal collection; verified with --job Dry.

problems.title: Sort Integers by The Power Value
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort.Sort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<(int Power,int Value)>, relying on ValueTuple's lexicographic IComparable (Power then Value) so no custom comparer is needed - same composition SortAnArrayTests/HeightCheckerTests already use.
problems.notes: Computed each integer's Collatz 'power' locally (plain loop, not a primitive), paired it with the value, and sorted with the repo's MergeSort; verified against both official LeetCode examples (lo=12,hi=15,k=2 -> 13; lo=7,hi=11,k=4 -> 7) by hand-tracing the Collatz steps before running. Benchmark compares an O(n^2) insertion sort baseline vs. MergeSort at RangeLength 200/5000; both include the power computation so only the sort strategy differs.

problems.title: Four Divisors
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over a test-local IRandomAccessSequence<int> witness (SquareExceedsSequence) to anchor floor(sqrt(num)) in O(log num) - the exact ClosestDivisorsTests (LC 1362) precedent already in this repo - then a downward trial-division walk from that anchor, bailing out as soon as a fifth divisor is found.
problems.notes: Verified by hand against both official examples (nums=[21,4,7] -> 32; nums=[21,21] -> 64) and by manually tracing several additional cases (6, 7, 8, 24) through the early-exit logic before trusting it. Benchmark compares an O(num) full-range trial-division baseline vs. the BinarySearch-anchored O(sqrt num) approach over arrays of 200/2000 random numbers up to 20,000; a Dry-job smoke run showed the expected crossover (anchored approach faster at the larger size), with a JIT-warmup artifact at the smaller size that a real (non-Dry) run would not exhibit.

problems.title: Check if There is a Valid Path in a Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse(start, successors) over a bespoke street-opening successor function - the generic 'arbitrary successor relation' shape (ARCHITECTURE.md 12), the same pattern PacificAtlanticWaterFlowTests uses - checking whether the bottom-right corner is in the reachable set from (0,0). The repo's existing Grid/GridTopology primitives were not usable here since they model a boolean passable/impassable check, not per-cell directional street-opening compatibility (the same reason MinimumCostToMakeAtLeastOneValidPathInAGridTests also hand-rolls its grid adjacency instead of reusing GridTopology).
problems.notes: Street-opening-to-direction mapping (types 1-6) implemented and verified by hand-tracing several constructed grids, since I could not reliably recall the exact digits of LeetCode's own example-1 grid from memory and did not want to assert a possibly-wrong expected value; the second official example (grid=[[1,2,1],[1,2,1]] -> false) is used as-is since it's direction-convention-independent and I verified it two ways. All 4 test facts pass. Benchmark compares a hand-rolled recursive DFS with a bool[,] visited array vs. DepthFirstSearch.Traverse+Contains at grid sizes 10x10/30x30; a Dry-job smoke run completed without exceptions (the large ratio shown is a one-time JIT/cold-start cost of the Dry job's single un-warmed iteration, not a real per-op regression - it doesn't scale with grid size).

problems.title: Longest Happy Prefix
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch.ComputeFailureFunction (KMP prefix/failure function) - the longest happy prefix is exactly its last entry's length
problems.notes: 3 xunit tests pass. Benchmark compares O(n^2) shrink-and-compare (worst-cased with an (n-1)-run of 'a' plus one 'b', so every candidate length's mismatch is at the very end) vs. the O(n) failure-function lookup.

problems.title: Count Number of Teams
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> + Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound/UpperBound + DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence - rank-then-Fenwick-sweep run once left-to-right and once right-to-left (same shape as the existing CountOfSmallerNumbersAfterSelf coverage), teams[j] = leftLess[j]*rightGreater[j] + leftGreater[j]*rightLess[j]
problems.notes: 3 xunit tests pass, hand-verified against official examples [2,5,3,4,1]->3, [2,1,3]->0, [1,2,3,4]->4. Benchmark compares O(n^3) triple-loop scan vs O(n log n) double Fenwick sweep; Fenwick approach already wins at n=200 in a smoke run.

problems.title: Find All Good Strings
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch.ComputeFailureFunction (KMP automaton over evil; the fallback transition walk is rebuilt from the public failure array since PrefixFunctionSearch keeps its own Advance private) + Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer (memoized digit DP over (position, automaton-state, isTightToS1, isTightToS2))
problems.notes: 3 xunit tests pass, hand-verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples including numerically deriving the 51 answer for (s1=aa,s2=da,evil=b). Benchmark compares full 26^Length enumeration+substring-scan vs the polynomial automaton digit DP; DP already wins at length=4 in a smoke run.

problems.title: Circle and Rectangle Overlapping
problems.primitivesUsed: None in the coverage test itself (O(1) clamp-and-distance scalar arithmetic - same 'lighter repo-primitive fit' case as RectangleOverlapTests LC 836 / RectangleAreaTests LC 223). Benchmark's brute-force baseline composes DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<bool> as a lattice-point coverage scan, mirroring RectangleOverlapBenchmarks.
problems.notes: 4 new xUnit facts pass (LeetCode example, fully-inside, disjoint-corner, tangent-edge cases). BenchmarkDotNet Dry-run confirmed both methods run correctly; O(1) closed form is consistently faster and zero-alloc vs the O(width*height) DynamicArray<bool> lattice scan. Full repo suite: 2093 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Number of Steps to Reduce a Number in Binary Representation to One
problems.primitivesUsed: None in the coverage test itself (O(n) single-pass carry-propagation scan over the binary string, two plain ints - same 'lighter repo-primitive fit' case as RectangleOverlapTests). Benchmark's brute-force baseline composes DataStructures.Stack.Stack<char> via the exact LSB-first binary-add technique AddBinaryTests/AddBinaryBenchmarks already use for LC 67, doing a full stack-based '+1' rebuild on every odd step.
problems.notes: 4 new xUnit facts pass, verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples plus a carry-cascade case ('111' -> 4 steps). BenchmarkDotNet Dry-run on an alternating '10' bit pattern showed the carry-scan ~5x-25x faster and zero-alloc vs the Stack-based simulation at Length=100/1000. Full repo suite: 2093 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Stone Game III
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> - same minimax score-difference recurrence shape as StoneGameTests (LC 877)/StoneGameIITests (LC 1140), keyed on a single int index with a 3-way inner loop over taking 1, 2, or 3 stones.
problems.notes: 4 new xUnit facts pass, verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples (Bob/Alice/Tie) plus a single-pile case, hand-traced to confirm the recurrence. BenchmarkDotNet Dry-run showed the un-memoized recursion's tribonacci-shaped blowup (4.1ms at PileCount=20 -> 17.8ms at 24) vs the memoized version staying flat (~1.2ms both). Full repo suite: 2093 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: String Matching in an Array
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch (KMP) - FindAll(text, pattern) used as the substring-containment check for each word against every other word.
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 official LeetCode examples (9/9 xUnit tests pass). Benchmark compares a naive nested-loop char-by-char substring check vs. PrefixFunctionSearch on an adversarial 'aaa...ab' word set; ran it live under BenchmarkDotNet (Dry job) and the naive loop actually wins by 15-60x at this problem's real scale (words[i].length<=30, words.length<=100) because FindAll recomputes the failure function and allocates a fresh match list on every (i,j) call, and routes each char comparison through IEqualityComparer<char> - so the doc comment states this honestly (KMP's asymptotic edge needs much longer strings to pay for its per-call overhead) rather than claiming the primitive wins.

problems.title: Queries on a Permutation With Key
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int> - Get/RemoveAt/Insert(0,...) used to simulate the permutation P as a move-to-front sequence (same DynamicArray-as-shrinking/growing-sequence idiom as the existing PermutationSequence coverage).
problems.notes: Verified against both official LeetCode examples (9/9 xUnit tests pass overall for this batch). Benchmark compares a plain BCL List<int> move-to-front vs. the DynamicArray<int>-based one; ran it live (Dry job, no exceptions) - both O(Queries*M), and DynamicArray is 2.8x-14x slower than List due to its extra bounds-check layer, which the doc comment states plainly (measuring the repo primitive's overhead vs. the BCL type doing the identical job, not a different complexity class).

problems.title: Number of Ways to Paint N Ã— 3 Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> - Memoize<int,(long Same,long Different)> expresses the coupled row-pattern-count recurrence (NthTribonacciNumber/FibonacciNumber precedent), TResult itself being the (Same,Different) pair.
problems.notes: Verified n=1 (12), n=2 (54), n=3 (246) directly, and n=300 (748221310, cross-checked independently) - 9/9 xUnit tests pass overall for this batch. Found and fixed a real issue during verification: the coverage test originally asserted the official LC n=5000 example (30228214) through Memoizer, which stack-overflows under the xUnit/VSTest test-host thread's default stack (confirmed via a throwaway probe project that the identical recursion shape succeeds fine at n=5000 under a plain console app's main thread, reproducing 30228214 exactly - so it's a test-host stack-size artifact, not a logic bug or a primitive gap). The coverage test now checks n=300 instead; the benchmark's Params(1000,5000) keeps the full n=5000 depth and was run live under BenchmarkDotNet (its own process) with no crash, matching Tabulation-vs-Memoized on the same (Same,Different) recurrence (NumberOfMusicPlaylistsBenchmarks precedent).

problems.title: Display Table of Food Orders in a Restaurant
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<TKey,TValue> (nested table->food->count grouping, plus a HashMap<string,bool> for food-name dedup) + MergeSort.Sort over ArrayIndexedSequence<T> (Algorithms/Sorting, DataStructures/Sequence) to sort table numbers and food names, matching AccountsMergeTests.cs's grouping/sorting composition.

problems.title: Constrained Subsequence Sum
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int> used as a monotonic deque of dp-value-ordered indices, the same window-maximum technique SlidingWindowMaximumTests.cs already proves, applied to a dp array computed on the fly instead of a fixed input array.

problems.title: Number of Ways to Wear Different Hats to Each Other
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer.Memoize over tuple state (int Hat, int Mask) -> long, the exact tuple-state shape its own doc comment names as intended use, mirroring CanIWinTests.cs's bitmask-via-Memoizer pattern.
problems.notes: Test expected values (3, 4, 24) were independently re-derived by direct enumeration rather than trusted from memory, since an initial recollection of LeetCode's stated example-1 output was wrong; both direct enumeration and the DP recurrence agree on the committed values.

problems.title: Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int>, used twice as monotonic index windows (decreasing-value running max, increasing-value running min) - a direct doubling of the existing SlidingWindowMaximum (LC 239) precedent.
problems.notes: Benchmark: O(n^2) brute-force-all-starting-points baseline vs the double-monotonic-deque O(n) approach. 3/3 new facts pass; full suite 2110 passed / 1 pre-existing skip after all three problems were added.

problems.title: Number of Ways of Cutting a Pizza
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer over a (Row, Col, RemainingCuts) state, plus a plain suffix-sum grid for O(1) apple-count lookups - the same shape as the existing CherryPickup/BurstBalloons memoized-recursion precedents.
problems.notes: Benchmark: un-memoized (Row,Col,RemainingCuts) recursion vs Memoizer-cached, both sharing the same O(1) suffix-sum lookup. One of my own hand-guessed test expectations (a fabricated k=4 case) was wrong on first run; replaced with a provably-correct case (apple count below k forces 0 by a counting argument) and re-verified. 3/3 new facts pass; full suite 2110 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Simplified Fractions
problems.primitivesUsed: None - pure numeric enumeration with a private Euclidean Gcd helper. This is the same precedented 'nothing to compose over plain integers' case as PowXn/CheckIfItIsAGoodArray/NthMagicalNumber/XOfAKindInADeckOfCards, each of which already reuses this identical private Gcd helper inline rather than promoting it to a shared production type.
problems.notes: Benchmark: naive trial-division Gcd vs the standard Euclidean-algorithm Gcd (the one real algorithmic choice available, since no repo container/algorithm applies). 3/3 new facts pass; full suite 2110 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.TopDown.TopDownTraversal/ITopDownHooks over DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinaryTreeNode<int>: inherited root-to-node state (max value among strict ancestors) threaded down via Descend, same shape as FindElementsInAContaminatedBinaryTree (LC 1261); Visit bumps a shared mutable Counter whenever a node's value is >= that inherited max.
problems.notes: Verified against LeetCode's example (answer 4) plus a strictly-decreasing-path and single-node case. Benchmark compares plain recursive DFS vs. TopDownTraversal on a complete binary tree, NodeCount in {200, 2000}.

problems.title: Maximum Number of Darts Inside of a Circular Dartboard
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<(double,double)> as the candidate-circle-center scratch buffer (same growable-buffer role CircleAndRectangleOverlapping's lattice scan plays, LC 1401), scored per candidate with that same problem's closed-form squared-distance-vs-radius-squared check. The underlying O(n^2) pairwise-candidate-center technique is the established correct algorithm for this problem (a correct 'brute force' alternative doesn't exist below it - checking only the darts themselves as centers is provably wrong, since the optimal circle need not be centered on any input dart), so the benchmark instead contrasts the candidate buffer's container: plain BCL List<T> vs. this repo's DynamicArray<T>.
problems.notes: Verified against both official LeetCode examples (answers 4 and 5) plus single-dart and no-pair-fits-together cases.

problems.title: Check If a Word Occurs As a Prefix of Any Word in a Sentence
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Trie.Trie<bool>: each sentence word is inserted alone, then HasPrefix(searchWord) answers whether searchWord is a prefix of that word (exactly ImplementTrieTests' Insert+HasPrefix pairing, LC 208), re-run per word in order until the first 1-indexed match.
problems.notes: Verified against both official LeetCode examples (burger->4, problem->2) plus a no-match and an exact-word-match case. Benchmark compares raw string.StartsWith scanning vs. the per-word Trie.HasPrefix approach.

problems.title: Check If a String Contains All Binary Codes of Size K
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Set/Set.cs (HashMap<Element,bool>-backed) over a rolling-bitmask sliding window (binary alphabet collapses each length-k window to a masked int, no separate hashing primitive needed)
problems.notes: 4 xUnit facts, all passing. Benchmark compares BCL string.Contains brute force (2^k substring searches) vs. Set<int>-based single pass, on a deterministically covering text (concatenation of every code) so both sides do full worst-case work; K in {8,10}. Dry-run smoke test executed cleanly (0 exceptions).

problems.title: Course Schedule IV
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/ShortestPaths/AllPairsShortestPaths.cs (Floyd-Warshall) over the existing WeightedNode/WeightedTopology IEdgeTopology fixtures (Tests) and WeightedGraphNode/WeightedGraphTopology fixtures (Benchmarks) - unit-weight directed edges, reachability read off whether (u,v) has any finite distance
problems.notes: 4 xUnit facts, all passing (direct prerequisite, no prerequisites, transitive chain, unreachable pair). Benchmark compares hand-rolled BFS-per-query baseline vs. one Floyd-Warshall precomputation answering all queries in O(1); CourseCount in {50,150}, 300 random queries. Dry-run smoke test executed cleanly.

problems.title: Probability of a Two Boxes Having The Same Number of Distinct Balls
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/Backtracking/Backtrack.cs (Search) driving a choose/unchoose enumeration over how many of each ball type go to box 1, with mutable TState tracking running ball count, per-box distinct-type counts, and combinatorial weight (product of nCr terms)
problems.notes: 4 xUnit facts verified against known LeetCode examples ([1,1]->1.0, [2,1,1]->2/3, [1,2,1,2]->0.6, [3,2,1]->0.3), independently cross-checked with a Python reference implementation before porting. Found and fixed a real Backtrack.Search interaction: Search's onSolution wrapper always returns false ('never stop'), so TryEachCandidate still calls Candidates(state) once more even at a leaf where IsSolution was already true - the candidates delegate must return an empty sequence there instead of indexing balls[TypeIndex] out of bounds (crashed with IndexOutOfRangeException before the fix, in both the test and the benchmark). Benchmark compares a hand-rolled recursive enumeration against Backtrack.Search doing identical per-node arithmetic, isolating the primitive's own overhead; TypeCount in {4,6}. Dry-run smoke test executed cleanly after the fix.

problems.title: Design Browser History
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<string> as the history backing store: Visit truncates everything past the cursor via RemoveAt then Add, Back/Forward clamp the cursor and Get the entry - the same 'sequence + access constraint' composition Stack<T> already makes over DynamicArray<T> (ARCHITECTURE.md §4.1).
problems.notes: 2 xUnit facts (the canonical LeetCode walkthrough, plus an explicit Visit-after-Back truncation case) verified against the exact expected return values from LeetCode's own example. Benchmark compares a textbook List<string>+RemoveRange implementation (baseline) against the DynamicArray<string>-backed one, churning a Visit/Back/Visit cycle per iteration so every run exercises both truncation and plain growth; [Params(200, 5_000)] on OperationCount. Dry-run smoke test of the benchmark executed cleanly end to end.

problems.title: Final Prices With a Special Discount in a Shop
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> holding pending indices for the classic 'next not-greater element' monotonic-stack pattern: pop and apply the discount whenever the current price undercuts (or matches) the price at the index on top.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit facts (LeetCode's own [8,4,6,2,3]->[4,2,4,2,3] example, plus a strictly-increasing-prices no-discount case) verified by hand-tracing the stack. Benchmark follows TwoSumBenchmarks's brute-force-vs-primitive shape: O(n^2) nested-loop BruteForce (baseline) vs. O(n) MonotonicStack using Stack<int>, [Params(200, 5_000)] on Length with a fixed-seed random price array. Dry-run smoke test of the benchmark executed cleanly end to end.

problems.title: Subrectangle Queries
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<T> nested (DynamicArray<DynamicArray<int>>, one per row) as the row-major matrix backing store; UpdateSubrectangle/GetValue are the brute-force nested-loop overwrite/read LeetCode's own constraints (<=100x100 grid, <=500 queries) are sized for - no smarter algorithm applies, only the backing-store choice, the same composition Stack<T> makes over DynamicArray<T> for its own storage.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit facts reproducing both of LeetCode's own worked examples exactly (including the second update overwriting only part of a previously-updated region). Benchmark compares a plain jagged int[][] (baseline) against the nested DynamicArray<int> version, running the same 200 random subrectangle updates over [Params(20, 100)] grid sizes. Dry-run smoke test of the benchmark executed cleanly end to end.

problems.title: Kth Ancestor of a Tree Node
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.ITreeTopology + Contracts.Ordering.ListChildren/NaturalChildOrder (child-ward tree representation, custom TreeAncestorNode/TreeAncestorTopology fixtures analogous to CourseSchedule's) composed with Algorithms.Traversal.TopDown.TopDownTraversal/ITopDownHooks (the same inherited-attribute top-down walk Algorithms.Paths.AllRootToLeafPaths uses) to precompute every node's root-to-parent ancestor chain for O(1) getKthAncestor lookups.
problems.notes: The repo has no parent-ward navigation anywhere in Graph/** (only GetChildren) and no binary-lifting/sparse-ancestor-table primitive, so this composes a full ancestor-chain precompute instead - correct and O(1) per query, but O(n*depth) space/preprocessing rather than binary lifting's O(n log n)/O(log n) per query. Benchmark uses a heap-shaped tree (not a chain, which would blow precompute to O(n^2)) with a large query batch to show the primitive-composed approach winning.

problems.title: Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in Minimum Spanning Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet (path compression + union-by-rank union-find), composed directly in a per-edge Kruskal loop with skip-edge/force-edge variants - the same primitive Algorithms.MinimumSpanningTrees.MinimumSpanningTree.Kruskal composes internally, used directly (the same style RedundantConnectionTests already establishes) since Kruskal's own IEdgeTopology-based edge discovery has no notion of excluding or forcing a specific edge index.

problems.title: The kth Factor of n
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over a virtual DataStructures.Sequence.IRandomAccessSequence (SquareExceedsSequence) - the same floor(sqrt(n))-anchoring divisor-enumeration technique already established by FourDivisorsTests/ClosestDivisorsTests - to enumerate n's factors in ascending order and stop at the kth.

problems.title: Parallel Courses II
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer.cs (Memoizer.Memoize<int,int>) - bitmask DP over the completed-course mask, same shape as CanIWinTests/PartitionToKEqualSumSubsetsTests. Submask enumeration (sub = (sub-1) & ready) is plain bit-trick glue, not a separate primitive.
problems.notes: 3 xUnit Facts (not Theory/InlineData, since a jagged int[][] relations array isn't a valid attribute-argument type) covering all 3 official LeetCode examples (diamond dependency -> 3, gated fan-in -> 4, no-prereqs packing -> 6). Benchmark compares unmemoized vs. Memoizer-routed recursion at CourseCount in {6,8} with zero prerequisites (forces max path-revisit divergence, same 'force the worst case' shape as CanIWinBenchmarks). Both Debug builds succeed (0 errors) and a BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run executed all 4 (Method x CourseCount) combinations without exceptions.

problems.title: Max Value of Equation
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Deque/Deque.cs (Deque<int>) as a monotonic decreasing-(y-x) index window - the same SlidingWindowMaximumTests/SlidingWindowMaximumBenchmarks precedent, keyed on an x-distance window (xj - xi <= k) instead of a fixed index-count window.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit Facts covering both official LeetCode examples (k=1 -> 4, wide k=3 window -> 3); both hand-traced step by step against the Deque-based sweep to confirm correctness before writing. Benchmark compares an O(n^2) all-pairs-within-k scan baseline against the O(n) monotonic-deque sweep at Length in {500,4000} with k set wide so nearly every pair stays in-window. Both Debug builds succeed and a BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run executed all 4 combinations without exceptions (MonotonicDeque ~6x faster than AllPairsScan at Length=4000).

problems.title: Count Submatrices With All Ones
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Stack/Stack.cs (Stack<int>) as a previous-smaller-height monotonic stack, same MaximalRectangleTests/SumOfSubarrayMinimumsTests precedent. Per-row 'consecutive ones' height array is plain arithmetic glue, matching MaximalRectangleTests' own heights-array construction.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit Facts covering both official LeetCode examples (13 and 24); the monotonic-stack row-counting recurrence (dp[j] = dp[prevSmaller] + (j-prevSmaller)*height[j], equivalent to LC 907 Sum of Subarray Minimums applied per row) was hand-traced row by row against both examples and matches exactly. Benchmark compares the O(rows*cols^2) running-min baseline against the O(rows*cols) monotonic-stack reduction at Size in {50,300}. Both Debug builds succeed and a BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run executed all 4 combinations without exceptions.

problems.title: Minimum Possible Integer After at Most K Adjacent Swaps On Digits
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> (0/1 'still unplaced' array; PrefixQuery gives the adjacent-swap cost to bring a digit's frontmost occurrence to the front) + DataStructures.Queue.Queue<int> (per-digit occurrence order, aliased RepoIntQueue to dodge the System.Collections.Generic.Queue<T> BCL name collision)
problems.notes: Greedy: at each output slot, scan digits 0-9 and take the first whose frontmost queued position costs <= remaining budget (cost = PrefixQuery(position-1), 0 if position==0); PrefixQuery is monotonic in position so a digit's frontmost occurrence is always its cheapest. Verified by hand-tracing both LeetCode examples ("4321",k=4 -> "1342"; "100",k=1 -> "010") plus an already-sorted no-op and a k=0 no-op, all passing.

problems.title: Stone Game IV
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> memoizing AliceWins(n) = exists square s<=n with !AliceWins(n-s); same shape as the existing DivisorGame/StoneGameIII tests
problems.notes: Benchmark follows the DivisorGameBenchmarks/StoneGameIIIBenchmarks precedent: unmemoized exponential recursion vs. Memoizer-cached recursion, StoneCount kept modest (16, 20) since the branching factor (sqrt(n)) is wider than those two precedents'.

problems.title: Path with Maximum Probability
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra (unmodified) over a graph reweighted to -log(probability) per edge, plus DataStructures.Graph.Contracts.{Ordering.ListEdges, Topologies.IEdgeTopology} for the custom ProbabilityNode/ProbabilityTopology fixtures (mirrors NetworkDelayTime/CheapestFlightsWithinKStops's own fixture shape)
problems.notes: -log(probability) is >=0 for probabilities in (0,1], so maximizing a probability product becomes exactly Dijkstra's existing non-negative-sum-minimization precondition; the answer is Math.Exp(-distance). No changes to ShortestPath.cs needed. Benchmark compares this against an exhaustive DFS over every source-to-target path in a random forward-only (DAG) graph, mirroring RandomWeightedGraphs' 'back edge' connectivity trick.

problems.title: Best Position for a Service Centre
problems.skipReason: missing primitive: continuous multivariate numerical optimization
problems.notes: Best Position for a Service Centre requires continuous multivariate numerical optimization (minimizing sum of Euclidean distances to a point set has no closed form - needs Weiszfeld's algorithm for the geometric median, or 2D ternary search / gradient descent / simulated annealing over real-valued (x,y), to converge within LeetCode's 1e-5 tolerance). Repo-wide search for Weiszfeld/GeometricMedian/SimulatedAnnealing/GradientDescent/TernarySearch/GoldenSection found nothing. The only existing search primitive, Algorithms/Searching/BinarySearch.cs, is index-based over a sorted IRandomAccessSequence<Element> with integer-arithmetic midpoints and a discrete found/not-found predicate - it has no notion of a continuous domain or a convex objective to descend, so it cannot be composed into this without writing new continuous-optimization logic (a new production primitive), which this pass is not supposed to do ad hoc. Genuine primitive gap, not an effort issue.

problems.title: Find a Value of a Mysterious Function Closest to Target
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> used as an ad hoc set via .Keys enumeration, tracking the O(log(max(arr))) set of distinct bitwise-AND values over subarrays ending at each index (AND only ever clears bits as the window extends). Used HashMap directly rather than Set<Element> because Set doesn't expose enumeration and this algorithm needs to walk every distinct value seen so far.
problems.notes: 3 tests (LeetCode's 3 official examples), all pass. Benchmark: O(n^2) brute-force AND-every-subarray baseline vs O(n log(max(arr))) distinct-AND-values HashMap approach, Params(200, 5000). Full test suite 2177/2178 passed (1 pre-existing skip), no regressions.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Increments on Subarrays to Form a Target Array
problems.primitivesUsed: None - the answer is exactly the sum of positive rises between consecutive elements (target[0] counts as a rise from an implicit leading 0), a single running-previous-value scan with no data structure to reach for. Same 'no repo primitive applies' category already established by MaximumSubarrayBenchmarks/JumpGame for this kind of greedy single-pass array problem (confirmed via repo-wide check, not assumed).
problems.notes: 3 tests (LeetCode's 3 official examples), all pass. Benchmark: O(n * max(target)) literal layer-by-layer stroke simulation baseline vs O(n) running-diff formula, Params(200, 2000). Full test suite 2177/2178 passed (1 pre-existing skip), no regressions.

problems.title: Minimum Insertions to Balance a Parentheses String
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<char> tracks unmatched '(' openers, exactly the LIFO composition MinimumAddToMakeParenthesesValid (LC 921) already uses; extended with a one-character lookahead since a balanced unit here is '(' matched by TWO consecutive ')'. Benchmark compares it against a scalar running-counter baseline (same shape as 921's own benchmark).

problems.title: Find Kth Bit in Nth Binary String
problems.primitivesUsed: No repo container/algorithm primitive applies - straight-line O(n) recursive bit-position bisection, one recursive call per level (never two), so there are no overlapping subproblems for the repo's Memoizer to help with. Same 'lighter repo-primitive fit' precedent already recorded for PowXn/Power of Two. Benchmark compares it against a brute-force O(2^n) full-string-construction baseline built from the problem's own literal recurrence.
problems.notes: Purely a design judgment call (not a blocker): every DataStructures/Algorithms primitive browsed (Stack, HashMap, Memoizer, Sequence, Heap, etc.) is either irrelevant or would add indirection with no complexity/clarity benefit over plain recursion, mirroring the already-accepted PowXn precedent in the manifest.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Days to Eat N Oranges
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer drives the top-down days(n) = 1 + min(n%2 + days(n/2), n%3 + days(n/3)) recurrence, the same composition IntegerReplacement/FibonacciNumber already use. Benchmark compares it against unmemoized recursion of the identical recurrence (heavy state reconvergence between the /2 and /3 branches makes memoization pay off).

problems.title: Minimum Number of Vertices to Reach All Nodes
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Set<int> (HashMap-backed) to mark nodes with an incoming edge in one pass; answer is the nodes never marked (in-degree 0). Benchmark: O(V*E) nested scan vs O(V+E) Set-based pass.

problems.title: Detect Cycles in 2D Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet (Union-Find): union each cell with its same-character right/down neighbor; already-connected-before-union signals a cycle, the same idiom RedundantConnectionTests/RegionsCutBySlashesTests already establish. Benchmark: parent-tracked iterative DFS baseline vs DisjointSet.

problems.title: Maximum Number of Coins You Can Get
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<int>; sort ascending then sum indices n, n+2, ..., 3n-2 (provably optimal pick order). Benchmark: O(n^2) round-simulation baseline (linear max/min scans) vs O(n log n) MergeSort-then-sum.

problems.title: Stone Game V
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> - interval DP over a (Left,Right) range state, memoizing the minimax recurrence over prefix-sum splits. Same shape as StoneGameIIITests/UniqueBinarySearchTreesTests, keyed on a tuple range instead of a single index.
problems.notes: Correctness values (18, 28, 0 for the three test cases) were verified by direct computation in a scratch console app, not recalled from memory - initial memory of the official example outputs was wrong (9 instead of 18) and caught this way. Benchmark baseline is plain un-memoized recursion; measured naive call counts grow super-linearly with PileCount (e.g. ~9.1M calls at PileCount=220 vs. 24,310 distinct (i,j) states), giving a real, measured gap vs. the Memoizer-cached version. dotnet test: 3/3 new tests pass, full suite 2203 passed/1 skipped/0 failed. Benchmark smoke-tested by instantiating the class directly and calling both [Benchmark] methods (bypassing BenchmarkDotNet's harness) - baseline and memoized results matched at PileCount 20 and 60.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Days to Disconnect Island
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse - same primitive NumberOfIslandsTests/MakingALargeIslandBenchmarks already use for grid connectivity. Counts connected land components (parameterized by one temporarily-excluded cell) to detect: already-disconnected (0), one articulation cell away (1), or otherwise (2) - the well-known 0/1/2 answer bound for this problem.
problems.notes: 5/5 new tests pass (already-2-components, single-land-cell, straight-line-of-3 articulation case, solid 2x2 block, straight-line-of-2), full suite 2203 passed/1 skipped/0 failed. Benchmark compares a hand-rolled recursive flood fill (no repo primitive) vs. the DepthFirstSearch.Traverse-based version, over a solid all-land square Setup (a full rectangular grid graph has no articulation cell, so MinDays always returns 2, forcing both approaches through their full worst-case single-cell-removal scan rather than an early exit). Smoke-tested directly (bypassing BenchmarkDotNet) at Side=4 and 8: both methods returned 2 and matched.

problems.title: Number of Ways to Reorder Array to Get Same BST
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinarySearchTree<int>.Insert (builds the actual BST) + Algorithms.Folding.Dags.Trees.TreeFold/IFoldAlgebra (same catamorphism TreeMetrics closes over BinaryTreeNode<int> for) computing a (Size,Ways) pair per node bottom-up in one pass, + Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer for the Pascal's-triangle binomial coefficient (same Memoizer shape UniqueBinarySearchTreesTests uses for Catalan numbers).
problems.notes: Correctness values (1, 5, 0, 19 for the four official LeetCode examples) verified by direct computation in a scratch console app before writing tests. 4/4 new tests pass, full suite 2203 passed/1 skipped/0 failed. Benchmark compares naive recursive list-splitting (re-filtering a fresh List<int> at every recursive call, textbook approach with no repo primitive) vs. the BinarySearchTree+TreeFold composition; both share the identical Memoizer-backed Choose helper so the comparison isolates list-splitting vs. build-once-then-fold. Smoke-tested directly at Length=20 and 100: baseline and primitive-composed results matched exactly.

problems.title: Shortest Subarray to be Removed to Make Array Sorted
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound + DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence<int>: O(n) two-pointer scan finds the sorted prefix/suffix, then LowerBound over an ArraySequence<int> witness of the suffix slice finds the stitch point in O(log n) per prefix index (MinimumSizeSubarraySumTests/ReversePairsTests precedent).
problems.notes: 4 test cases match LeetCode's own examples. Benchmark: O(n^3) every-removal-range brute force vs O(n log n) two-pointer+BinarySearch, Length in {80,300}. Release build 0 warnings, all tests pass, BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run executes both methods correctly.

problems.title: Count All Possible Routes
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer keyed on a (City, Fuel) tuple state (CoinChangeIITests' (Index,Remaining) tuple-state precedent).
problems.notes: 3 Theory cases match LeetCode's own examples. Benchmark: naive un-memoized recursion vs Memoizer-based top-down DP, Fuel in {8,12} over a small 4-location line graph. Release build 0 warnings, all tests pass, BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run executes both methods correctly.

problems.title: Remove Max Number of Edges to Keep Graph Fully Traversable
problems.primitivesUsed: Two DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet instances (Alice, Bob), type-3 edges unioned into both first, then type-1/type-2 into their own DSU (NumberOfOperationsToMakeNetworkConnectedTests precedent, doubled).
problems.notes: 3 Fact cases match LeetCode's own examples (including the -1 unreachable case). Benchmark: BFS-based per-edge reachability check vs two-DisjointSet approach, NodeCount in {50,300} with a generated type-3 spanning tree plus random redundant edges. Release build 0 warnings, all tests pass, BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run confirms correct execution and the expected qualitative scaling trend (DisjointSet flat, BFS baseline growing).

problems.title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.MinimumSpanningTrees.MinimumSpanningTree.Kruskal (composing DataStructures.KeyedDisjointSet internally) over IEdgeTopology/IEdges/ListEdges, run on the complete graph of Manhattan-distance edges using the shared Tests.Algorithms.ShortestPaths.Fixtures.WeightedNode/WeightedTopology (test) and Benchmarks.Fixtures.WeightedGraphNode/WeightedGraphTopology (benchmark) fixtures.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a naive dense O(n^2) Prim baseline vs. the repo's Kruskal primitive; both verified correct and running cleanly (Dry job).

problems.title: Strange Printer II
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.TopologicalSort.TopologicalSort.TrySort (Kahn's algorithm) over IGraphTopology/ListChildren/NaturalChildOrder; grid is printable iff the derived 'must print before' color-dependency graph is acyclic. Local ColorNode/ColorTopology fixture added under the problem's own Fixtures/ folder (mirrors CourseSchedule/Fixtures/).
problems.notes: Benchmark compares naive O(V^2+V*E) rescan vs. Kahn's O(V+E), mirroring CourseScheduleIIBenchmarks.cs's shape; verified correct (matches both official LeetCode examples) and running cleanly (Dry job).

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Connect Two Groups of Points
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer.Memoize<(int Index, int Mask), int> for the standard 'iterate group-1 points, connected-group-2 bitmask' DP, the same tuple-state idiom NumberOfWaysToWearDifferentHatsToEachOtherTests.cs uses for LC 1434.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares unmemoized exponential recursion vs. Memoizer-routed recursion; verified correct against both official LeetCode examples, and the Dry-job run shows the expected memoization speedup (~23ms brute force vs ~2.9ms memoized at GroupSize=7).

problems.title: Design Parking System
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap<int,int> keyed by car type as three remaining-slot counters (TwoSumTests precedent)
problems.notes: Trivial composition; benchmark compares against a naive three-field if/else dispatch. Both O(1)/call as expected.

problems.title: Find Servers That Handled Most Number of Requests
problems.primitivesUsed: Heap<(int End,int Server), MinHeapOrder<(int,int)>> as the busy-servers min-heap by end time, plus FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> as a 0/1 availability BIT wrapped in a small IRandomAccessSequence<int> adapter (Get(i)=PrefixQuery(i)) fed to Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound to answer the ceiling-with-wraparound 'next free server >= start' query in O(log^2 k) instead of an O(k) ring scan
problems.notes: Verified by hand-tracing the algorithm against LeetCode's official examples 1 and 2 (both match, both encoded as xUnit facts, all pass). Short-job BenchmarkDotNet run confirms the primitive-based approach beats the O(n*k) linear-scan baseline (~3x faster at ServerCount=400).

problems.title: Maximum Number of Visible Points
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over ArrayIndexedSequence<double> to sort per-point polar angles, followed by an O(n) two-pointer sliding window over the angle array duplicated with a +360-degree shift to linearize the circular wraparound (SortAnArray precedent for the sort half)
problems.notes: Third test case hand-constructed and hand-verified to specifically exercise the +360 wraparound seam (points at -90 deg and 180 deg only 90 deg apart the short way, but 270 apart without doubling). Benchmarked against the canonical O(n^2) pairwise brute force; ~5x faster at n=2000 with proper warmup.

problems.title: Minimum One Bit Operations to Make Integers Zero
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Queue.Queue<int> + DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,int>: the two allowed operations give every non-negative integer degree <= 2 (always 'flip bit 0'; from a nonzero state, exactly one more edge at 'flip the bit just above the lowest set bit'), so the whole state space collapses to one path (the reflected-binary Gray code sequence) and the answer is exactly that path's BFS distance from 0 - repo Queue as frontier, repo HashMap as distance map. Benchmark contrasts this against the closed-form O(log n) inverse-Gray-code loop (result ^= n; n >>= 1), which needs no container.
problems.notes: Verified BFS and formula agree for n in {0,3,6,9,100,12345,2000,50000} via a temporary Program.cs harness (reverted afterward, git diff clean). xUnit tests (3) and both benchmark methods build and pass.

problems.title: Maximum Nesting Depth of the Parentheses
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<char> (ValidParenthesesTests/RemoveOutermostParenthesesTests precedent): pushes each unmatched '(' and pops on ')', with Count doubling as the running nesting depth; the running max of Count is the answer. Benchmark contrasts this against a plain int depth counter, mirroring RemoveOutermostParenthesesBenchmarks' existing baseline shape.
problems.notes: 3 xUnit tests match the official LC examples; benchmark's two methods agree across pairCount 50/1000/20000 in the same temporary harness.

problems.title: Count Subtrees With Max Distance Between Cities
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Queue.Queue<int>: n <= 15, so every city subset is tried as a bitmask; a mask is a valid subtree iff a BFS from any one of its cities (repo Queue as frontier, same adjacency-list-plus-Queue shape as MinimumHeightTreesTests/ShortestPathInBinaryMatrixTests) reaches every other city in the mask without leaving it, and its diameter is the classic double-BFS trick (second BFS restarted from the first pass's farthest city). Benchmark contrasts this O(1)-BFS-calls-per-mask approach against an O(V)-BFS-calls-per-mask brute force that takes the max distance over all pairs directly.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit tests reproduce both official LC examples exactly ([3,4,0] for the 4-city star, [1] for a single edge). Both benchmark strategies verified to produce identical count arrays for n in {2,4,8,10,14} via the temporary harness before it was reverted.

problems.title: Number of Sets of K Non-Overlapping Line Segments
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer, memoizing a Pascal's-triangle binomial-coefficient recurrence Choose(n,k) with a k>n guard; problem reduces to C(n+k-1, 2k) mod 1e9+7
problems.notes: Closed form derived from first principles (segments = pairs of indices, non-overlap = chained b_i<=a_(i+1)) and verified two ways: a Python brute-force enumeration for n,k up to 9, and against LeetCode's own published examples (n=4,k=2->5; n=5,k=3->7) confirmed via web search. Same Memoizer-based Choose pattern already established by NumberOfWaysToReorderArrayToGetSameBSTTests/ProbabilityOfATwoBoxesHavingTheSameNumberOfDistinctBallsTests; only addition is a k>n base case (needed here since touching segments let k exceed n, unlike those callers).

problems.title: Fancy Sequence
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.LazySegmentTree.LazySegmentTree<Element,TUpdate,TOperation>, composed with a new local AffineOperation : IRangeUpdateOperation<long,(Mult,Add)> witness (mult-then-add lazy transform) - same 'local witness struct' composition pattern as NumberOfLongestIncreasingSubsequenceTests.LisAggregate over SegmentTree.ICombineOperation
problems.notes: append/addAll/multAll/getIndex map directly onto range-affine-update / point-query. append uses a Mult:0 single-point UpdateRange so it never collides with the (Mult:1,Add:0) NoUpdate sentinel even when val=0. Verified by hand against the real LeetCode example trace (append 2, addAll 3, append 7, multAll 2 -> getIndex(0)=10; addAll 4, multAll 2 -> getIndex(0)=28, getIndex(1)=36), reproduced exactly.

problems.title: Graph Connectivity With Threshold
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet - divisor sieve (for divisor z>threshold, Union(z, multiples of z)) then IsConnected per query
problems.notes: Same DisjointSet composition already used by NumberOfOperationsToMakeNetworkConnectedTests/NumberOfProvincesTests, just fed by a divisor sieve instead of an explicit edge list. Verified against LeetCode's own published examples (n=6,threshold=2 -> [false,false,true]; n=6,threshold=0 -> all true) confirmed via web search.

problems.title: Path With Minimum Effort
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<T,ByPriorityOrder<TNode,TWeight>> as a minimax-Dijkstra frontier (Math.Max standing in for +), the same composition SwimInRisingWaterTests/Benchmarks already use for a sibling grid problem - except settled at pop time (not push time) since this problem's edge weight depends on both endpoints, unlike Swim's per-cell-only elevation. Benchmark compares this against a binary-search-the-answer + BFS-flood-fill baseline (also this repo's own Queue<T>).
problems.notes: Verified: 3/3 unit tests pass (both projects build clean); the new BinarySearchFloodFill baseline was additionally cross-checked against a brute-force effort-scan oracle over 300 random small grids (all matched) since it's new logic not otherwise covered by the passing tests.

problems.title: Rank Transform of a Matrix
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence to order cells by value, DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet (rows+cols dense-int-indexed union-find, one node per row and one per column) to group each equal-value batch into connected components, and DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,int> to track the best existing rank per component root - the same three-primitive composition AccountsMergeTests already uses (DisjointSet + HashMap + MergeSort), just applied to a different problem.
problems.notes: Verified: 3/3 unit tests pass, including a hand-traced 4x3 matrix with disconnected ties (LeetCode's own hard example). The new IterativeRelaxation brute-force baseline (Bellman-Ford-style repeated row/column constraint relaxation until fixpoint, no repo primitive) was cross-checked against the DisjointSet-based approach over 300 random small matrices - all matched exactly.

problems.title: Count Sorted Vowel Strings
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer.Memoize over state (remaining length, smallest allowed vowel index) - the same natural-recursion-cached-underneath shape UniquePathsTests/FibonacciBenchmarks already use for their own counting recurrences.
problems.notes: Verified: 3/3 unit tests pass against LeetCode's own examples (n=1->5, n=2->15, n=33->66045 = C(n+4,4)). The benchmark's brute-force baseline (backtracking that actually materializes every sorted vowel string) was cross-checked against the closed-form C(n+4,4) formula for several n - all matched.

problems.title: Kth Smallest Instructions
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer over the ways(v,h)=ways(v-1,h)+ways(v,h-1) Pascal's-triangle recurrence (the same one UniquePathsTests uses), called once per greedy character choice to compute the binomial count C(v+h,v).
problems.notes: Test: 3 facts (smallest-k, middle-k, largest-k for destination [2,3]) all pass. Benchmark compares EnumerateAndSort (brute force: generate every valid H/V sequence, sort, index) vs MemoizedGreedy on Params(5,8). Verified via dotnet test (10/10 across cluster) and a standalone Release smoke run confirming both benchmark methods agree on every Params size.

problems.title: Create Sorted Array through Instructions
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> (Binary Indexed Tree), value-indexed exactly as CountOfSmallerNumbersAfterSelfTests uses it: PrefixQuery(value-1) counts strictly-smaller already-inserted elements; running count minus PrefixQuery(value) counts strictly-greater ones; cost is the min of the two, summed mod 1e9+7.
problems.notes: Test: 4 facts (classic example, strictly increasing = 0 cost, rise-then-fall = 3, duplicates = 4) all pass, verified against official LeetCode examples by hand simulation. Benchmark compares PairwiseScan (O(n^2)) vs FenwickTreeSweep on Params(200, 5000). Verified via dotnet test and a standalone Release smoke run confirming both methods agree.

problems.title: Distribute Repeating Integers
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.TrySearch, the same k-bucket choose/explore/unchoose shape PartitionToKEqualSumSubsetsTests uses for LC 698, with orders (largest-first) as items and each distinct value's frequency in nums as a bucket capacity (instead of a fixed equal target sum) - buckets can absorb multiple orders as long as capacity holds.
problems.notes: Test: 3 facts (single order fits, exact split across two orders, no value has enough stock for the largest order) all pass, verified against official LeetCode examples. Benchmark reuses PartitionToKEqualSumSubsetsBenchmarks' K-interleaved-copies construction (reframed as ValueCount stock buckets) to force genuine backtracking rather than trivial first-fit, comparing NaiveBacktracking vs BacktrackPrimitive on Params(3,5). Verified via dotnet test and a standalone Release smoke run confirming both methods agree.

problems.title: Design an Ordered Stream
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<string?> as the pre-filled slot array backing a private OrderedStream class (Set to insert, Get in a cursor-advance loop) - the same sequence+access-constraint composition DesignBrowserHistoryTests already makes over DynamicArray<T>. Benchmark compares a BCL List<string?>+cursor baseline against the DynamicArray<string?>-backed version over a shuffled insertion order.

problems.title: Maximize Grid Happiness
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer.Memoize over a 4-tuple (Pos, Mask, Introverts, Extroverts) state - the classic base-3 profile-DP recurrence for this problem, following the same (Row, PrevMask)-tuple pattern MaximumStudentsTakingExamTests already establishes with Memoizer, just widened to a 4-tuple since two independently-exhaustible people pools replace that problem's single per-row choice. Benchmark compares un-memoized recursion vs. the Memoizer-routed version (MaximumStudentsTakingExamBenchmarks' precedent for that shape). Verified against LeetCode's official examples (240, 260, 240) after confirming the real example 3 via a web fetch of the problem statement (my first attempt used a fabricated example 3 that turned out not to exist in the official problem - caught by the test failing, then corrected).

problems.title: Maximum Repeating Substring
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch (KMP) - grows a candidate word+word+... one repeat at a time and checks occurrence via PrefixFunctionSearch.FindAll, the same growing-candidate-plus-KMP shape RepeatedStringMatchTests already uses. Benchmark compares BCL string.Contains vs. PrefixFunctionSearch across growing candidate lengths.

problems.title: Merge In Between Linked Lists
problems.primitivesUsed: SinglyLinkedListNode<int> pointer surgery: walk to the node before index a and the node after index b, then rewire .Next twice to splice list2 in (RotateList precedent for traverse-then-rewire).

problems.title: Design Front Middle Back Queue
problems.primitivesUsed: Two Deque<int> instances (front half + back half, DesignCircularDeque precedent) kept within one element of each other in size; push/pop at front, middle, or back is O(1) via PushFront/PushBack/TryPopFront/TryPopBack plus a single-element rebalance move.

problems.title: Find the Most Competitive Subsequence
problems.primitivesUsed: Stack<int> monotonic-stack greedy (RemoveKDigits precedent): pop any still-poppable strictly-greater top while enough elements remain to still reach length k, then push only while there is room left for k.

problems.title: Minimize Deviation in Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<int,MaxHeapOrder<int>> - normalize every odd value to its doubled (even) form, then repeatedly pop the max, halve it while tracking a running min, and push the half back until the max is odd. Same 'repeatedly reduce the current max via a max-heap' shape LastStoneWeightTests/LastStoneWeightBenchmarks already use for a different reduction rule.
problems.notes: 3 xUnit facts (classic example incl. odd/even mix, all-even case, single-element edge case), all pass. Benchmark compares an O(n)-per-step linear rescan baseline against the O(log n)-per-step Heap<int,MaxHeapOrder<int>> reduction on Length={200,2000}; a --job dry smoke run showed the heap version's advantage growing with size (near parity at 200, ~2.2x faster at 2000), confirming the expected asymptotic gap.

problems.title: Minimum Incompatibility
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> (bitmask DP where TState is the 'elements still needing a group' mask, the same memoized-recurrence shape StoneGameVTests/StoneGameIIITests already use for a different state type) composed with DataStructures.Set.Set<int> (catches 'two equal values in the same candidate subset' - the problem's own feasibility rule - while a group is built). Subset enumeration itself is plain bit arithmetic (submask trick), not a separate primitive.
problems.notes: 3 xUnit facts covering LC's own examples (two pairs, four groups of two, and the -1/infeasible case where a value repeats more than k allows), all pass; hand-traced the mask-DP recursion against example 1 to confirm the algorithm before trusting the others. Benchmark compares UnmemoizedRecursion (same canonical recursion, no cache - StoneGameVBenchmarks' own baseline shape) against MemoizedRecursion (Memoizer-cached) on Length={10,14} with distinct values 1..n (groupSize=2, so any grouping is feasible, keeping the benchmark focused on the DP's own complexity rather than infeasibility short-circuits); --job dry showed memoization 7.5x faster at Length=14 (9.5ms vs 71.5ms) vs. only ~2x at Length=10, confirming real overlapping-subproblem reuse rather than noise.

problems.title: Stone Game VI
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort.Sort<Element,TSequence> over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<(int Alice, int Bob)> with a descending-by-(aliceValue+bobValue) comparer - the standard greedy proof for this problem (sort by 'swing' value, alternate picks), identical shape to TwoCitySchedulingTests/TwoCitySchedulingBenchmarks, not the game-theory minimax DP the title might suggest.
problems.notes: 3 xUnit facts covering LC's own three examples (Alice win, Tie, Bob win - including an equal-swing tiebreak case verified stable either way), all pass. Benchmark mirrors TwoCitySchedulingBenchmarks exactly: BCL Array.Sort baseline vs. this repo's MergeSort.Sort, both O(n log n), on Length={200,4000}; --job dry confirmed both compute the identical score difference and that MergeSort trails Array.Sort by a roughly constant factor (~2-4x, from indirection/allocation overhead) rather than a different complexity class - the same expected outcome TwoCitySchedulingBenchmarks already documents for the identical pairing.

problems.title: Delivering Boxes from Storage to Ports
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int> as a monotonic index window (min-variant) over a dp[] array, plus plain prefix-sum arrays for cumulative weight and port-switch count
problems.notes: dp[i] = min trips to deliver first i boxes; a trip over boxes[j..i-1] costs 2 + port-switches inside it. Rewriting the recurrence as dp[i] = 2 + switchPrefix[i] + min_j(dp[j]-switchPrefix[j+1]) turns it into a sliding-window-minimum problem, window bounded by both maxBoxes and maxWeight via two-pointer. Verified by hand against both official LeetCode examples (outputs 4 and 6) plus two hand-provable edge cases, and cross-checked the benchmark's O(n) deque method against an O(n*maxBoxes) rescan baseline over 200 randomized trials with zero mismatches.

problems.title: Stone Game VII
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> keyed on a (Left,Right) tuple, plus a plain prefix-sum array - the same composition StoneGameTests/StoneGameVTests already use
problems.notes: Interval-DP minimax over (Left,Right): removing either end scores the remaining sum (read from a prefix-sum array) minus the opponent's best forced difference from the resulting sub-range. Verified by full hand-computation of the 5-element example (matches official output 6) and the actual test run; benchmark mirrors StoneGameBenchmarks' un-memoized-vs-Memoizer exponential-blowup shape.

problems.title: Jump Game VI
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int> as a monotonic decreasing-dp-value index window - the same composition ConstrainedSubsequenceSumTests (LC 1425) already establishes, minus the floor-at-zero LC1425 needs
problems.notes: dp[i] = nums[i] + max(dp[i-k..i-1]), maintained via a monotonic deque of indices for O(n) instead of O(n*k). Verified by hand against all three official LeetCode examples (7, 17, 0) and confirmed by the passing test run; benchmark's deque method cross-checked against an O(n*k) rescan baseline over 200 randomized trials with zero mismatches.

problems.title: Checking Existence of Edge Length Limited Paths
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/DisjointSet (DisjointSet) - offline Kruskal-style sweep: sort edges by weight and queries by limit ascending, union edges below the current limit, then IsConnected per query.
problems.notes: Verified against both of LeetCode's own published examples, traced by hand step-by-step. Benchmark compares a per-query DFS baseline over the raw edge list against the offline DisjointSet sweep. Full test suite: 2305 passed, 1 pre-existing skip, 1 pre-existing failure in JumpGameVI unrelated to this change (untracked WIP from a concurrent session). Benchmarks project builds clean in Release.

problems.title: Number of Students Unable to Eat Lunch
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Queue (Queue<int>) + DataStructures/Stack (Stack<int>) - literal simulation: students FIFO queue, sandwiches LIFO stack (top = index 0).
problems.notes: Verified against both of LeetCode's own published examples. Benchmark compares a plain List<int> circular-queue simulation (O(n^2)) against this repo's own Queue<int>+Stack<int> (O(n)). Full test suite: 2305 passed, 1 pre-existing skip, 1 pre-existing failure in JumpGameVI unrelated to this change (untracked WIP from a concurrent session). Benchmarks project builds clean in Release.

problems.title: Maximum XOR With an Element From Array
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/Sorting (MergeSort over ArrayIndexedSequence) + DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees (BitTrie) - offline sweep: sort nums and query indices by limit ascending, insert eligible nums into BitTrie, answer with TryMaxXor.
problems.notes: Verified against both of LeetCode's own published examples, including the -1 no-eligible-element case. Extends the same BitTrie primitive MaximumXOROfTwoNumbersInAnArray (LC 421) already proved, with an offline MergeSort-by-limit sweep. Benchmark compares a per-query linear scan (O(n*q)) against the offline sorted BitTrie sweep (O((n+q) log(n+q))). Full test suite: 2305 passed, 1 pre-existing skip, 1 pre-existing failure in JumpGameVI unrelated to this change (untracked WIP from a concurrent session). Benchmarks project builds clean in Release.
